OFFICE is like When a man gets a taste of it once, he lee ever afterwards has a hankering for it. "Is there any kind of coat that never has any buttons on it ?' asked a mission teacher of a class of newsboys. "Yes, sir; a coat of paint has nary a button, was the instantaneous reply. i'Vneer old Mrs. Oravedown read about the ere- mating of a score of human bodies, she exclaimed: "Only to think of such goings on? It is a burning shame!" You've Jingleson professed to have been out on a lark, but it was believed by those who saw him come home that he had really been out on a Swallow. "Tug American eagle still screams !" thundered a silver coinage orator, holding up a silver dollar so the crowd could see it. " LOU bet he does," came a voice from the multitude; "he 3creama for the other fifteen cents." A NEWLY-MARI:IED LADY was telling another how nicely her husband could write. "Oh, you should see some of his love-letters!" "Yes. know," was the freezing reply; "I've got ever au many of 'em in my desk." A EETTING-3IAN sat and watched with interest and excitemeut the perpetration of a violin and piano duet. "A dead heat, by dove !" he ex- claimed, as both instruments womul up at the same time. A CONCEITED man, of the name of D'Oyley, hav- ing said that he wished to be called De Oyley, somebody at dinner (says Moore) addressed Imn the,— " Mr. De Oyley, will you have some De-umpling ?" Tits latest rumour concerning the infallitaity of Doeton speech relates to the owl. It is said that the common, igorant owl of the rest of the country says "'To whit, to whoo," but the cultivated owl of Boston says "To whit, to whom." "Wire is a nomination to public office so often called an empty honour, father ?" asked a boy of an old politician. " Because, my son," was the solemn reply, "it rarely fails to empty the pockets of the victim of the nemieation." "DON'T you suppose," said a member of the police force, "that a policeman knows a rogue when he sees him ?" "No doubt," was the reply; "but the trouble is that he does not seize a rogue when he knows him." " Leuna," said Mrs. Parvenu, on the hotel piazza, to her daughter, "Laura, go and ask the leaders of them orchestras to play that sympathy from Meddlejohn ' over again; it's such an awful favourite of mine and your father's, too I" SCENE-Art school. Mrs. Nouveau—" And is that large picture some of your work?" Pupil— " Mine ? Oh, no, madam l That is one of the old masters." Mrs. Nouveau, in an undertone to her companion—"l don't like to hear a young man speak so disrespectfully of his teachers.

" YEs, eald Mrs. Snags, "I left my husband at home to take care of the baby while I went to the theatre. He didn't sly anything much when I came home, except that I never looked so hand- some to him, but I found the next day that our parrot had learned some horrible, horrible words."

A YOUTH, ambitions of acquiring pugilistic skill, some time ago waited upon a professor of the "noble art," with the intention of taking lessons. "Now what do you consider the best posture of defence ?" asked the aspiring young hero. " Why, to keep a civil tongue in your head," was the judicious reply. I HAVK heard (says Lord William Lennox) of a post-prandial speaker who, wishing to pay a com- pliment to the land of his birth, shouted out— " England is an island—England is an island ;" then, forgetting the fervent eulogium he was about to make, abraptly concluded by saying, "and long may she remain so." Lenv—" I am so glad to make your personal acquxintance ! I have often read your name." Poet, flattered—" Ah ! Do you know my lyric poems or my novels V Lady—" Neither." Poet —" My tragedies ?" Lady—" ; bet, yeti see, you happen to live in the same house as a friend of mine and whenever I visit her I see your name on the door-plate." , AT a parochial examination the minister asked a sort of half-crazy woman what love was, which tke string of his former questions led him to. " What's love, Nanny ?" "Hoot lye, sir," says Nanny, " dinna spear sic daft-like questions as that, when I'm sure ye ken that love's joust an unco lykin.sa mind ; an' what mair can me or ony other body say about it?" A romeous individual going up the staircase of a large hotel was violently poked in the back with an umbrella by a man who ran after him. When he turned to ascertain the cause of the assault, the other saw the mistake and apologized, saying : "Excuse me, sir; I thought you were my old friend Brown." "Indeed !' said the old gentle- man, in measured tones "and does your old friend Brown enjoy this sort of thing ?" "Doceroa, I wish you would prescribe for my husband." "What ails him, madam ?" "That's what I don't know. Whenever I ask him for a new bonnet, or anything of that kind, he is very hard of hearing; but when I try to go through his pockets in the morning, the lifting of his trousers wakes him from a sound sleep." " If your husband is deaf, ma'am, I think I can cure him." ONE morning Henry Compton, the famous actor, and Douglas detrold proceeded together to view the pictures in the"" Gallery of Illustration." On entering the ante-room, they found theraselves opposite to a number of very long looking-glasses. Pausing before one of these, Compton remarked to Jerrold :—" You've come here to admire works of act ! Very well, first feast your eyes on that work of nature !"—pointing to his own figure reflected in the glass—" look at it; there's a picture for you'!" "Yes," said Jerrold, regarding it intently, "very fine, very tine iimeed !" Then turning to his friend :—" Wants hanging though !" THOSE (says Lord William Lennox), who liked a witty remark, or a pungent epigram, would join the table at which James Smith sat, and any com- monplace remark of the day was immediately com- mitted by him into verse. I remember once asking him if he was going to the ball at the Mansion House, got up in aid of the ucfoitunate Polish refugees. "No," said he. Than, calling for a sheet of paper and a pencil, he wrote the follow. jug lines ; " Aloft, in rotatory motions hurled, The poles are called on to support the world. In these our days a different law controls ; The world is called on to siipport the Poles." WHILE at a revival meeting an old lady happened to sneeze, and as nearly every eye in the house was turned towards her, immediately after she had sneezed, she felt very aecornfortable. When she had arrived at home, she said to Dinah, her w coloured maid-of-all-work, ho had accompanied her to the meeting, "Dined', why didn't you take the blame of that sneeze on your shoulders? You should have niade it appear as though it was you, not I, that sneezed." At the revival the next evening, the old lady i happened to sneeze again. The preacher paused n his discourse, and there was a slight titter among the congregation, which increased to a roar as the simple-minded but honest Dinah arose; and remarked, "I takes de blame of dat sneeze dat my reissue hab jest sneezed on my own shoulders." MR. HAYWARD tells how a Frenchman, dining With an Englishman let drop the remark, "I ea a great deal of bread with my meat." "Yes," was the reply, "and a great deal of meat with your bread.

Mr. Salmon, in the new number of "The Strand Magazine," gives a striking description of a service at the Deaf and Dumb Church in Oxford-st. The visitor finds himself in the midst of a congregation which gives expression to the prayers through the fingers, which sings hymns by signs, which follows a sermon not a word of which is spoken aloud, and which assembles in a church without an organ and without a choir. For two hours every Sunday morn- ing and evening there is a service,during which not a sound, save a cough, or whisper from the altar, is to be heard.

These are eight in number, and form an interesting collection, which it is intended shall be exhibited in the tea room of the House of Commons shortly after the Chancellor of the Exchequer has been enabled to communicate to the House the recommendation of the Committee. At present he awaits signification of her Majesty's pleasure.

The flight of the Royal Family to the Riviera seems anything but prudent in face of the preval- ence of influenza there. A trustworthy correspon- dent informs us that the epidemic of influenza is bo alarming at Cannes and Nice that there is quite an exodus therefrom of British residents, who have crossed the Italian frontier to Dr. George Macdon- ald's favorite resort, the pretty little town of Bordighera, which, although not free from the grippe itself, has had to turn people away from its hotels. To add to the danger of this severe scourge a cutting March wind sweeps over the Riviera just I now.

Sweet are the use§ of electricity. At a dinner- dance given in Washington a few days ago to the son of the American President, Mr. Russell Harri- son—the young gentleman who once described himself as " same rank as the Prince of Wales, you know "—the guests ate under a canopy of green dotted with electric lights of every hue. Great balls of roses hung above their heads ; and when the feast was over Mrs. Russell Harrison pressed an I electric button and the rose balls burst and showered themselves over the belles and beaux who occupied the thirty-six places about the table. Heliogabalus had his rose feast,and why not the son , of the Chief Magistrate of the more or less United I States ?

Even emperors, it appears, have to recognise the stern law of necessity. They can make vulgarly boastful speeches and prosecute unoffending news- papers, but sooner or later they have to open their eyes to widespread distress. It is therefore better to hear late than never that the Emperor of Ger- many, who recently talked those wild words about pursuing his own course, has secured reports from all parts of the empire regarding the possibility of finding work for the unemployed and that the central committee in Berlin for providing work is now busy trying to find work elsewhere for the unemployed. These remedial measures are, so far as they go, good, but it is to be feared that they do not go very far.

We may expect some charming results from the Australian tour of Mrs. H. M. Stanley—Dorothy Tennant. This clever artist excels in depicting street arabs and boys generally,and has found some models entirely to her taste in New Zealand.So much so that she has publicly stated that the Dunedin boys were "the sturdiest and rosiest-cbeeked chil- dren she had ever seen." Apropos of artists, Miss Chamberlain, daughter of Mr. Josept Chamberlain, M.P., is devoted to flower painting, which she is now studying assiduously with Mrs. P. H. Miller, who, as Miss Sophia Holmes, exhibited in Dublin so many beautiful groups of flowers, painted from nature just as they were growing. Mrs. Miller is a pupil of Sir James Linton.

-- Mr. Joseph Skipsey, whose new volume of "Songs and Lyrics" has just been published, attained his reputation late in life. For forty years he worked in the Northumberland mines, but as he wielded the pick he also "hammered the ringing rhyme," and now " the mad world hears." It was Mr. Edmund Gosse who'" discovered" him; and through theinfluence of his new friends he was appointed curator of Shakespeare's House three or four years ago. He found no satisfaction, however, in Strat- ford-on-Avon ; and he has turned his back on the place. He lives now in his native Northumbria, and there he will end his days. The miner poet has a remarkable appearance. He has very bright eyes which look out beneath shaggy, overhanging brows; a mane of grey. hair; and an air of thought- fulness which marks his poetic vein,

Mr. Wolff, who on Monday night took his seat in the House of Commons for East Belfast, shares with Sir Edward Harland a distinction that as no parallel in the present Parliament, and for which no one can recall a precedent. He is a member of the eminent shipbuilding firm of Harland and Wolff, and both the principals have seats in the House ot Commons.

Mr. Gustav Tuck, now the senior partner in Messrs. Raphael Tuck and Sons, is a pleasant man of somewhat florid complexion, with dark hair and moustache. He is the son of the original Raphael Tuck, and to his wonderful business tact and energy the almost unique position of the firm is due. The run on the "Queen's Letter" will be enortnous. Messrs. W. H. Smith and Sons estimate that their sale will be about six thousand a day.

The Emperor William's recent extravagances and aberrations, which have so troubled his family and entourage, are attributed at Court to the fact that his ear malady has been very troublesome lately,and he has suffered many paroxysms of the most excrucia- ting pain. This ailment appears to be getting worse, for the attacks now recur with increasing frequency, and, as it is pronounced to be iucurable, the conse- quences are likely to be most selious.

-- I regret to bear that Sir W. llarcourt's eyesight is now in so unsatisfactory a condition .that the gravest apprehensions are entertainedby his friends. Sir William has been troubled about his eyes for nearly two years past, and more than eighteen months ago be went to Wisbaden for several weeks in order to consult the oculists there. lam sorry to learn that the eminent specialists who have lately been consulted have not given a very favourable re- port of the case.

Dr. Joachim was asked in the artists' room at the last St. James's Hall Popular Concert why it was he showed so little sympathy with the admirers of a certain cantatrice, celebrated for her wonderful ex- ecution of roulades, &c., " What would you have ?" said the great violinist. " Here have 1 been all my life endeavouring to imitate on my violin the ex- quisite tones of a human voice ; this singer, on the contrary, only seeks to imitate my violin. We can never please ourselves."

Principal Cairns, one of the leading theologians in Scotland, died at Edinburgh on Saturday. It is only a week or two since he resigned his posi- tion as Professor of Systematic Theology in the United Presbyterian Church College. Principal Cairns was a famous preacher and a cultured scholar. his contributions to philosophic thought and his works earned him a reputation as a writer and thinker. }le was born in Berwickshire in 1807, studied at Edinburgh and Berlin, and joined the United Presbyterians as a minister in 1867.

The Hon. and Reverend Willisam Rice, who has been appointed to the living of Great Yarmouth, is a son of the late Lord Dynevor, who was himself rector of Fairford, in Gloucestershire. Mr. Rice is a very hard-working and zealous clergyman, who has labored arduously in the East-end of London. Yarmouth is remarkable as having furnished his first curacy to the Rev. Lord William Cecil, second son of the Premier, who, being familarly known by the sobriquet of "Fish" Cecil, was most appropri- ately selected for a cure in the great bloater borough.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH l9, 1892. IN A NEW ENGLAND VILLAGE. (con!iuded.)
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH l9, 1892. IN A NEW ENGLAND VILLAGE. (con!iuded.)
BY H. WHITHAM.

I arrived in Worcester on a clear and crisp frosty Sunday morning. All the stores were closed ; busi- ness of all kinds was at a standstill. No saloons,no cigar stores with great open fronts, or coloured lithos, were to be seen. It seamed as if I had fallen suddenly upon another planet. A sweet repose filled the air. Instead of that indescribable and in- tolerable hum to which I had been used,there was a calm that could almost be felt. Had I dropped again into dear old England? Was I once more wending my way up Manchester-road? It needed but one thing to be added for all to be real : church bells ought to have pealed out a welcome, and the illusion would have been complete. Heine has said somewhere "that the industrial portion of the Eng- lish community bear the outward stamp of reli- gion." This is well borne out in Worcester amongst the native population, the inward stamp being a religion that consists in a sense of individual sub- ordination to the greater interests of humanity,and in loyalty to eternal laws. ARRIVED IN GREENDALE,

..... a small village of some few hundred inhabitants, I was immediately put at rest by the kind and hearty welcome I received. What if I was surrounded by frost and snow, did it not remind me of an English winter. I had yet to experience its rigours, which were anything but English " don't-cher-know." The first evening I attended church (we have .no chapels here), as in duty bound. Was it not a Latch- ford boy who was to preach, and had I not already had a shake of his hand,and heard his clear English voice ring out a-welcome to Greendale The ser- mon I may not criticise, but the preacher with his health and strength beaming through his happy looking eyes,seemed,somehow or other, to stand out and away from the usual pinched, and over-anxious look ot the American. I did enjoy myself thoroughly sitting in the church, sometimes listening, and, I am afraid, quite as often allowing my attention to wander, and my mind to fasten itself upon the scenes and doings of other days. Most of your readers will know' the Latchford Radical, Mr. Luke Ellison. His work in the cause of temperance, and his readiness to at all times give a -helping hand to all meliorative measures has made him a well- known figure amongst the reformers of Warrington. For me to meet his son,Joseph Ellison,and to find him the ordained pastor of the Baptist church here, was indeed a pleasure. Like most of the ministers here, he is enthusiastic in the cause of total abstinence, and, if I may say so, seeks to make a speciality of its ethics for the guidance of the young,feeling that the peculiarly catholic doctrine of gaining the young cannot be used in a better cause than tem- perance. For myself the difference in the two places, where I did live, and where I do live, was so great that I soon made my mind up as to what I should do.

high class are set before the members, and public lectures on current questions, scientific and other- wise, are attended to by special committees. Ad- joining this hall is a moderate-sized one, let off for lodge purposes and to the School Board; children are thus familiarised with the building. Descend- ing to the basement is a fine airy gymnasium—just splendid in its fittings, &c. To finish all, swimming and tub-baths are provided. Leaving out the gymnasium,all these inducements to lead an honest and sober life may be had for the mere sum of Sc. per year. If American workmen and her capital- ists can once be brought to grasp the full meaning of the eight hourc question, can once be brought to see the criminality of working and being forced to work, from Monday morning early until six o'clock Saturday evening, America would be the El Dorado of not only her workmen, but of their pastors and masters.

div.head: ARTIFICIAL COLOURING OF FLOWERS.
div.p: ARTIFICIAL COLOURING OF FLOWERS.

To paint the lily used to be considered a wholly superfluous labour, but it seems from the communi- cation of Mr. Brockbank in "The Gardeners' Chroni- cle" that the horticultural world is just now in great excitement about the artificial colouring of flowers, which, as we have lately noted, is said to have been accidentally discovered by a young workgirl in Paris. Yellow daffodils, it is announced may be " beautifully striped with dark scarlet in twelve." The secret is simply that of dipping their stalks in aniline dye dissolved in water to about the transparency of claret. Readers of Shakespeare and Herrick will probably prefer nature's honest gold. Indigo carmine, we are assured, also produces " beautiful blue tints." The two combined dye various shades of purple, with curious mottled effects, some parts of tho flowers becoming pink and other parts blue and purple. Greens are pro- duce by using the blue dye with yellow. Indigo and cochineal have been tried with partial success. Lily of the Valley flowers became tinged with pink or blue in six hours ; Narcissi are changed from pure white to deep scarlet in twelve hours, delicate shades of pink are imparted to them in a very short time, and so forth. It is fair to say that our horticultural contemporary certifies to thopractical utility of these processes in showing the coarse of the juices of the plants. This in the case of tulips enables the grower to distinguish the varieties much earlier than he would otherwise be able to do. With all respect to Mr. Brockbank, this seems really all that can be honestly said in favour of " the artificial colouring of flowers."

" Newbery House Magazine," for March,publislied by Messrs. Griffiths, Farran, and Co., is more than, usually interesting. Amongst the subjects, dealt with are " The Clergy Discipline Bill," " Disestab- liehment," Cardinal Manning (with portrait), Arch- bishop Trench's Petry, Church Folk-lore, &c. We take several extratts from the last-named paper. Referring to the custom of dividing the sexes in church, the writer says That the usage was common in Cambridgeshire the following incident will show. On one occasion, the curate of a parish in that county stopped during his sermon, as some one was talking, and said, "I hear a noise." The occupant of a seat on the women's side, of the church said, "Please, sir, it is not us." Curate :- " I'm glad to hear it; it will be the sooner over." "I remember when 1. was a boy," writes a gentleman from Abingdon, "a young couple coming into the church here on a Sunday afternoon and seating themselves to- gether on the women's aide. The man was soon turned out of his seat by the verger, with the remark, uttered in an audible voice, We don't have no sweethearting here.'"

his always gratifying to find a man who has the sense to tell a good story against himself. A clergyman has put the following upon record : "Nearly forty years agie.,about 1850—I officiated amongst a simple people on the borders of Worcestershire and Herefordshire, where the practice of bowing to the altar was not uncommon ;- but to me, a young clergy- man, from the neighbourhood of London, it was novel, and I imagined myself to be the object of reverence. I remonstrated with an aged parishioner, who gave me to understand that the revereuce was made to the Almighty, not to a fellnw-sreature. Her decided manner at the time is vividly impressed upon my mind. A neighbeer to whom I recently related the anecdote, remarked that , the same mistake was once made by H.E.H the late Prince Consort, and that it met with a similar rebuff." Everybody is imthe habit of saying, or appearingdso say, some sort of brief prayer upon taking his place in church. lam told that formerly an old man in a parish in Yorkshire used to say his preparatory prayer facing round in turn to each corner of his pew. Is it possible that this queer usage was some how connected with itte Ad familiar formtfA : "Matthew, Mark, Luke. and John, Bless the bed that I lie on. Four corns to my bed. Four AngclS round me spread, Two at focii; and two at head. And four to carry me when I'm dead l"

div.head: GRENADIER AND HIS POTATOES.
div.p: THE GRENADIER AND HIS POTATOES.

An interesting anecdote of the first Napoleon is related in a letter from a correspondent, who was a considerable time in the French military service, and who vouches Tar its authenticity. The evening before the battle of'Ulm, when Napoleon, in cons- . .

, pony with Marshal Berth*, was walking incognito through the camp, and listening te the talk ,of his sAdiers, he saw ii:oagroup not far off a grenadier of the guard. who was roasting some!potatoes-in the ashes. "1 shoulcV like a roast potato above all things," said the Emperor to the Marshal; " ask the owner of them if he will sell one. In obedieneo to the order,Berthieradvatteed to the group and, asked to whom the potatoes belonged. A grenadier step- ped forward and said "They are mine." "-Will you sell me one ?:' "Il have only Jive, and that'A. hardly enough for my supper.' "I will give., you two Nispoleons if yon,wilirsell me one." "I don't want your gold: I shelb be killed, perhaps, to•morrow, and I don't warty the enemy to find me with an. empty stomach.." Berthier reported, the sol- dier's answer to, the Emperor, who • was stand- ing a little in the background. "Lt's, see if I shall be luckierrthan you," said the latter, and, going up close to,the grenadier, he asked him if he would sell him,a.potato. "Not by along shot," said the grenadier ;,"Ilhaven't enough for tnyps,lf." "But you may set your own price. Come,larn hungry,and haven't eaten to-day." "I tell you 'haven't enough for myself ;; besides all that, do you think I don't know you in spite of your disguise?" "Who am I, then ?"• "Bah!! the 'little cornoral,' •as they call you; am, I' right ?" "Well, since .youltabow me,will you sell me a potato ?" "No.; : but if you would have me come and dine with you when you get back. to Paris, you, may sup with meto-night." " said Napoleon," on the word of 'a little corporal:, on the word of an Emperor." "Welland good. Oox potatoes ought to be done by, this time ; there are the two largest ones, the rest 111'eat myself." The Emperor sat down and ate his potatoes, and then returned with Berthier to his, tent.., merely remerleo ing, " The rogue is a good soldierifil wager." Two months afterwards Napoleon, the, Great was in,the, midst of a brilliant court at the palace of the "I'nil- leries,and was lust sitting down. to dine,wh en word was brought him that a grenadine was without try- ing to force the guard at the dcor,saying that hehad been invited by the Emperor.. "Let him come said hie Majesty. The soldien entered, presented arms, and said to the Emperoci "Do you remember once having supped with me off my roasted note, toes?" " Oh, is that you.?? Tee, yes, I remember:* said the Emperor; "and, salyou have comet° dine. with me, have you Rustan, lay another- cover on. your table for this brave fellow.' Again the grena- dier presented arms, and said: " A grenadierof the guard does not eat with lackeys. Your Alajpty told me Ishould dine with you—that was the bar- gain, and trusting,to yourword,l have come hither.' "True, true," said the Emperor," lay a coves- here near me ; lay aside your arms, mon anti, and draw up to the table." Dinner over, the grenadier went at his usual pace, took up his carbine, and turning to the Emperor, presented arms, and said "A mere private ought not to dine at the ta.ble of his Emperor." " Ah, I understand you," said Napoleon. "I name you Chevalier of the Legion of Honour and lieutenant of my company of guards. "Thank you heartily;, rive! Rovereur !" answered the soldier, and withdrew,

div.head: I AM NOW A TEETOTALER,
div.p: I AM NOW A TEETOTALER,

and am determined, if health permits, to do some little for the cause. It is the rule throughout America, at least it is wherever I have been, that workmen's clubs and trade unions shall not under any pretence be held in any building where intoxi- cating liquors are sold. In all the trades meetings I have attended I have never once seen business interrupted through the bringing in of drink. Only once have I seen a man partially intoxicated in the meeting, and he was ordered out. What a differont tale could I tell of my own union at home ! Au! and of others there, where the first hour, and that the most sober, is almost always lost, through the bringing in of liquors. This partially applies also to Friendly Sozieties. Years ago I spoke against the meeting in public-houses of these societies. To my view it was prejudicial in two ways. It helped to make and to keep men drunken, and it compelled parents, who had their children's welfare at heart, to forbid their entrance into these otherwise dem-- able societies. I say nothing of the impossibility of freely and fairly discusing the important subjects coming before a trades union linden uch conditions. lam no believer in force. If a majority, having the power, force the minority, good results rarely follow. It was Lincoln who said, "some of the, people may be wrong all the time; all the people may be wrong some of the time; but all of the people are never wrong all of the time." I suppose some of the people here must be wrong now; but on the let of March they will have to bow to the majority. A vote of the whole of the adult people of both sexes has been, taken, and after that date the sale of liquors will be illegal. I have noticed, that, as 'things are, liquor shops are not at all numerous, and these are compelled by law to take more the appearance and duties of restaurants than of the ordinary gilded saloon. The traffic in drink is subject to an ever watchful magistracy, and a policeman suspected of being in collusion with the publican would soon find his occupation gone. Of course, notwithstanding all these precautions, there is a deal of quiet drinking,' and in the back streets what are called kitchen dives thrive. The drug stores have a deal to answer for, many of these be- ing nothing less than blinds for the sale of liquor. Every day amusing reports come round of some one being detected having peculiar and ingenious apparatus for supplying the thirsty customer. This is

HOW THEY DO IT AT FALL RIVE. "An extraordinary liquor raid was made at Fat River, Wednesday evening. When the officers were about ready to give up, Officer Medley founds false cupboard containing a string which appeared to work some kind of hidden machinery. The five men tore down the partitions- and worked their way into a cellar 18 feet deep and then chopped through into a sub-cellar whose bottom was 10 feet lower. Here they found a lead pipe leading into a bank of earth, in which they found a large, empty, wooden box. They learned that the suspicious lead pipe went through the iron pillars supporting the build- ing, but they searched vainly for barrels. They found that the string in the cupboard worked a heavy block of wood two feet square. When the bar-tender pulled the string the block fell upon some mechanism that shut off the beer in all of the pipes and caused water to run through them. The police- men discovered portions of two barrels of ale, a quantity of hard liquors and some wines. While- they were laboring nearly 1000 people were attract- ed by the excitement. The most of the piping in the cellar and neighbourhood of the building was used as a decoy and must have cost almost as much as a small cottage hones." I have heard of men spending several thousands of dollars in fitting up premises for the sale of liquor, only to be disap- pointed when the annual voting time came round in' January. One cannot but think that the profits must be immense to justify 1 business men in such a risky expenditure. If fOrce.,l is not to be used, and we are told moral suasion is I a failure, naturally the question arises, what other] course is open? 'Veil, the two forces may be com- bined, so working reformers may feel satisfied when, they look round. Certainly, in Massachusetts, it I would be impossible to disgrace the magistrates' bench with a man whose wealth, whose family's wealth, was the direct outcome of a whole district's disgrace. It would be a moral impossibility for the head cf a great brewing firm to sit, year after year, in the 'nation's parliament, making laws to restrain the criminal he himself had helped to make, I have said Reformers may be satisfied with their work. Of course I only refer to England, for which I have statistics by me; I have not been able to get them for the States. Thirty years age the number of short term prisoners was 20,833; now they are something like 13,076. Years ago, I, along with others who dabbled in ink, and yet more practical work, felt assured that it was in the school house that the start in real reform must be made, and the credit in England is due to a Gladstone Govern- ment, and the untiring energy of W. E. Forster. More can yet be done. SINCE I CAME TO WORCESTER,

--- I have seen much that has gladdened my heart. The I city is proud to own its relationship with the old Worcester of England. .It has pleased the citizens to hold out the right hand to the Mayor of its Eng- lish namesake. It has done this and more without dreading the foolish charge of Anglo-mania which some of the press, through sinister motives, see fit to throw around. Walking through the city, I was invited to look through the Young Men's Christian Association. I did so, and I never in all my life saw anything like it before. The arrangements for the oomfort of members, and visitors, are simply per- fect. If the institution does not make it more easy to do right, than it is to do wrong, why I think the ingenuity of man need be no further taxed. We must confess to being beaten, A large, well-carpeted, well-furnished room opens to the visitor as soon as he enters. Tables are scattered about for draughts, and ' chess. All the English and American serial litera- ture is there; and several pianos stand ready for the musically inclined. Going upstairs we find a hall as large, or larger, than your own Public Hall and a deal better fitted up. In this hall theatricals of a

THE CURSE OF THE CALLERLEYS.
By LILLIAS WASSERMAN, Author of "Some Fisher Folk," "Judith," "Where the North Wind Blows," &c., doc.

CHAPTER XXIL TrrE BIRTH OF AN HETR. After that evening in the churchyard, Lady Callerley became almost as moody and reserved as her husband. Had the latter not been self- absorbed he must have noticed the change. How at on% time she would cling to him, a great pity and tenderness filling her wistful eyes; and how at another she would shrink away suddenly as though some horror interposed between them, which she dared not brave. _ _ _ _

But Sir Lancelot had been a bachelor for too longaperiod to havelthe whole tenour of his thoughts and ac,tions changed completely by the slight epi- sode of matrimony; more especially since he chose to regard Silvia as a child, a toy, a plaything and to consider that to ask her to share his anxieties and burdens would be to take an unfair advantage of her youth. Had the passion which reduces old and young to the same level of folly (or wisdom?) mastered -his judgment, no such scruples, be sure, would have hindered him from claiming his wife's sympathy ,- and together, heart and soul, any sorrow and any fear may be faced by those that love truly. But the sweet unreason, the endearing selfishness, the exactingness which knows no con- tent, the cruelty, bitter from excess of yearning; all these attributes of love were things as yet un- known to Sir Lancelot _ .

Silvia came nearer to' the comprehension of love's mysteries; and because of this, perhaps, her hus- band's studied care of her met with scant gratitude. A woman would rather be ill-used from love and jealousy, than she would be treated with perfect justice, if juatice be only another word for in- difference. The knowledge that she was obliged to hide from him made her appear cold and undemon- strative; and changed her from a child, careless and light hearted, to a woman who gave little and expected less in the way of sympathy. Madam watched her, as a cat does a mouse, to use Bell Widdrington's simile; and settled within her own mind that since fate was working to please her, she might safely rest.on her oars ,a little, and note how the tide flowed. Sir Lancelot consulted her once abortt Silvia's depression and silence, but the experienced wife and mother laughed at his solicitude, and prophesied smooth things; and he rested satisfied,. relying upon her superior wisdom, . Upon a wild night in Deeember, when the wind was howling round Seaton Callerley as though all the ghosts and. witches in the world were flying and sailing abroad upon it, and yelling to be allowed entrance; an heir was born to Sir Lancelot. A pretty boy, with great blue eyes like those of his mother, and more definite features than generally fall to the lot of infants. To Madam's astonishment, Lady Callerley got through her trial extremely well. Perhaps Mrs. Breamish forgot to make sufficient allowance for youth and intense vitality. At any rate if that lady bad cherished hopes, which -were to say the least of it extremely inhuman, they were certainly doomed to disappointment. Everything un- pleasant was forgotten by Silvia in the supreme bliss of motherhood. AIL the misgivings and fears and horrors of the preceding months were swept away as utterly, as though they had never existed, by the flood of rapture that rushed over the young mother, and filled her whole being, at the corning of her Loy. There was no room left for aught save love and joy and supreme contentment. It was Bell Widdripgton who first noticed' that, fine handsome child A the newcomer undoubtedly was, there were symptoms, about him that told of some pre-natal.mischief ; symptoms doubtless the effects of the intense. nervous excitement from which his mother had been suffering for the past few months. He slept much too lightly and for too short perioda, and his big eyes had occasionally a strangely startled look in them, painful to see in a baby-face. Mrs.-. Posset, the nurse, a large moon- faced Woman, with an enviable belief in her 'own capabilities and wisdOm.i. pronounced him a perfect . paragon of babies (a phrase, which from being re- peated to each successive mother in rotation, had become to her a necissary formula, and ours that never lost its effect), and.added that it wasiextra- ordinary the notice he took, and so wonderful, that he might have been in the world before ! engagement at a distant part of the county hag prevented her acceptance of the fair Dorothy as a ' patient. The ways of Providence are aggravating weys.at times, even to a well-regulated Christian mind; and it was a source of constant irritation 'Co the good woman, who had a proper pride in her efficient skill, that this chance proved the sole one. Why on earth should not the *leer creature have gone on, like ordinary women and increased the population annually, to the pleasure and profit of a sully unappreciated person; who got tired of the whims and fancies of little chits, such as her present patient, chits totally unfitted by nature and disposition to be mothers; since they were not con- tent to abide by the wisdom of age and experience, to, say nothing of lawful authority. So it came to pass that Madam was in high favour, ada that Mr& Posset even deigned to con- sult her occasionally as to the relative value of various old-fashioned syrups and cordials. ordained for the soothing and curing of infantile disorders. And Madam smiled sweetly and yoke with a silver tongue, while rage and envy and hatred filled her heart _ _

It only needed Sirvia's little burst of triumph the first time they met, to put the finishing-touch to the devil's work going on within Mrs. Breamish's "We- are equal now," cried the new mother from her downy ;test among the pillows, " you have -a boy, and I have a boy—only I have a little the best of it, since mine is the heir to.Callerley." "While mine bids fair to, become heir to beg- gary;" answered Mrs. Breamish, carefully con- cealing her Inger. "Never mind Silvia- there are always dsaw-backs,and I amcontent 1 Let us be friends !"

Lady Callerley's blue eyes looked np dbubtfully. She was too happy now to hate anyone. If Madam really wished for peace, it seemed mean to keep up perpetually this undercurrent of hostility? She could now understand much better how Madam must naturally have hated anyone who came between her boy and his prospects. Really, considering this, it was superhumanly :pod of her to hold out the olive branch. Silvia felt penitent. Nature was teaching her to be large hearted. .She laid her hand upon. the strong, firm, white one lying near it. "1 have been provoking. It is nice of you to forgive. Kiss me, Dorothy, and love my boy for his father's sake."

Just for one moment Dorothyßreamish hesitated. So might Judas have paused before he 'crowned his sublime treason with a, kips.. "For his fatirr's sake !" And that steeled her heart again at once. The father who was not father of her boy, but of Silvia's. Sha stooped and gave. the asked for kiss.

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MARCH 19, 1892.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MARCH 19, 1892.

the bodies of the two children. Both were lying face downwards, with their little bodies simply covered with a night shirt, and with their legs perfectly bare. 'lite first body taken out was that of a boy about five years of age. Ile wore a striped print shirt, and his head was wrapped in what appeared to be a piece of old linen. When the body was takes up the stench., which previ- ously had been quite intdierable, now became infinitely worse. Those present dared not breathe unless they wentti, a window to do.so, and every window in the house was thrown open. The body of the first child discovered was immediately taken upstairs into one of the bedrooms. When the head wrap was removed it was discovered that not only was there a fearful wound on the head, but the throat had been cut and nearly severed from the 'body. The remains were dreadfully decomposed. 'The body of a 'fair-haired little girl of truout seven years was next brought out. Her throat also had been terriely cut. After 'removing the bodies of 'two children the police began to excavate the body of the woman, +alio it now became apparent was deeply embedded in the cement. Slowly the work proceeded, but ultimatifly one foot peeped above the earth. It was covered with a soft house Shoe. Then the figure became Apparent, brit it was only in outline. Great difficulty was foundin extracting the body, as it was so firmly fixed in the cement. It was seen that the woman :had a rope mend her neck, the ends of which were cut sharply dif as if she had been hanged and cut down. A policeman tugged at the rope, but it gave way and the digging operations commenced again, the body being ultimately removed. While the men were at work dig- ging round the body of the woman, they made the unex- peeted discovery of the body of a baby girl lying at the foot athe woman. Soon afterwards a fourth child, a girl of about ten years, was found lying beside the woman. The body of the woman was wrapped in an eider down quilt, and tied lightly round with a rope. She was fully dressed, with the exception of a boot and stocking on one foot, all her clothes being of a very tine quality. She had on a print morning dress. The throat was cut. She was of a very dark complexion and had short black hair, suggestive of her being half-taste. On her left hand 'was a wedding ring and keeper. All the bodies were in,an advanced state of decomposition, and the work of getting them out was completed only 'after great difficulty. The burial of the bodies had been carried out in a very systematic and complete manner. A deep hole had been dug and the bodies of the woman and two children placed in it, the cement being poured upon them. Two ,of the elder children were then placed in the hdie and more cement poured on them. The flags were then laid 'upon the top of the hole, and over all was a layer of six inches of cement which extended over the entire-kitchen '(On the removal of the last of the bodies they-were all laid out in the upper room, and work was discontinued for the day. The police, however, entertain the belief ' thatno more bodies were interred in the kitchen.

CAN HE BE "JACK THE RIPPER'?" The greatest excitement prevailed in Raithill and neighbourhood,a,nd wildest rumours were afloat as to the other missing females, who it was stated had visited Williams and had not been seen since. These-stories are being inquired into by the police. Many people, who knew Williams when he was in Rainhill, believe that he will be found to be no other than " Jaek'the Ripper." One-important fact in this connection is that tie notori- ous Whitechapel murders commenced about the time Williams was supposed to have first arrived -inlEng,land, and that since July la.st,when William § put man appear- ance at Rainhill, there have been no more East End out. rages of that description. It has been discovered that the cement used in the Denham Villa was purchased from Messrs. Howarth and Co., St. Helens, whose ledger contains: "To theorder of Miss Mather, Rainhill, July 23, one barrel of cement, 'August 1, one barrel ;and August 4., one barrel." The barrels were fetched by Oliver Duxbury, son Of the land- lady of the 'Coach and Horses Inn, RainhilL, and 'were paid for when taken away. The police have taken pos- session of the portmanteau which Williams left' behind him- at the hotel, and which bears inside:traces of what are apparently blood stains. It is stated that Williams did his best to get into society atßainhill and Fluyton, but although be dis Played gold and diamonds in profusion, they were not sufficient recommendation.

THE MARRIAGE TO MISS MATHER. There was a curious circumstance about the marriage of Miss:Mather which has not gone unnoticed. Towards' the end of August Williams gave it out that holwas going to travel abroad for a considerable time, and it being .understood that he was bound for India, and that he would return in. the spring to claim his bride-Tor good, a banquet was held at the Commercial Hotel, towhich the leading residents of the place were invited. The follow- ing is a copy of the invitation card issued on that occa- sion :—Mr. Albert.O. Williams requests the pleasure of the company of-- at a social banquet at Mr. 'E. H. ,Shores Commercial Hotel, Rainhill, on Wednesday, August 26i 1891. previous to his departure from Rain- kill. at 7.30 p.m. The evening will conclude with toasts, addresses, songs, &e." The card was artis- tically got up, and on the folded wings at the .back was the silvered initial." W." in conspicuous lettering. A very happy evening was spent, and the health of the future couple was duly pledged in flowing bunrpers. It was arranged that another banquet would be laeld at the same hostelry when the bridegroom returned. -He duly took his departure, but it was believed he never went further than,Liverpool, and he turned up again very unexpectedly at the village, when the marriage was hastily pushed on. ,A singular feature of the proceeding was that Williams did not take his bride to the villa in Lawton-road. •After the marriage the pair proceeded to New Brighton ,and subsequently to the South. of England. Withanas had lareviouslY disposed of the furniture he had purchased in Liverpool, by private sale. The banquet at •the • Com- •nlereial was not settled for,, but he agreed to tet the land- lord take some things in part payment of the bill, .and a dining table, some chairs, and a bed, ostensibly purchased for the.principal—Colonel Brooks—were accepted irr this .way, the balance being handed over in cash. Some- thing.; was alleged as to the great-expense to whichiColonei ,-Brooks was put, and so the villa was broken up. It is stated that Williams had a lot of heavy beGes.at . the villa and these he wished :to have removed. HO spoke to the landlord of the Commercial Hotel about them; and he offered to take them away. but in the meantime, Williams engaged . a tradesman ,trf St. Helens to do the workoand they were somewhat ciandestinely removed: Cellrat they contained was never 'hnown. • Williams left at. the Commercial Hotel two leather travelling ,bags, one of the Gladstone type, anti the other a ‘portmanteau. These, in the light of the reYela- ,aans recently made, have been w...rowly scruti 'fbe portmanteau has the maker's label "Scott Brothers " distinctly impressed on it, but the place of. the manufacture has teen scratched out with a !pen- kore. Th.veare traces of sealing we at the apertures as-if the portmanteau Lad contaicaedeurnething of great , value. Inside there are stains applrently of bleed. 'Various partly-eff aced relway labels refer to Liverpool, Hull, and other places. There are aZzo some 'Masonic kigns4rtside. According to a further report from Australia, it is stated that, in addition .to the hady..c.l Miss Mather, vribictifiaas been discovers, a woman ard two children had :been missiec for some time. If these cases be con- neertedwith Wikams, they bring up thetatal number of murders to nine.

div.head: WHOLESALE MURDERS AT RAINHILL.
div.p: WHOLESALE MURDERS AT RAINHILL.
'FIVE BODIES FOUND BURIED IN AWILLA. GHASTLY DETAILS.

The quiet little village of Rainh ill, near-St. Helenk which isepon the London and North-Western Rai way route, and is known as being the locale of thq +County Lunatic Asylum, was on Wedneeday throwit into a state of intense excitement by the discovery that murders on a wholesale scale had v•been perpe- trated in its midst. On Saturday last a telegram from Melbourne stated that the body •ef a woman, 1 the victim of a cruel murder, had been Idiscovered in I an empty house in Windsor, a subarbSif Melbourne; horiedom cement under a fireplace in one of tee rooms. It happened that the housekeeper of Mr. , Short had a friend in that troop, and she very natur- ally supposed that Williams would know the name of the colonel, probably be an acquaintance of her friend. She questioned him upon the sub- ject, but he returned an abrupt ard evasive answer, and did not allude further to the subject. To make up for any deficiency in this respmt Williams made a great point of displaying a number of warlike trophies of which he had become possessed in the course of his wanderings and engagements. He had what is described as a large quantity of 1 war tackle," poisoned daggers, and other implements. These are now in the possession of a villager at Rainhill, and are shown as curious mem- entoes of the strange mysterious man. On one occasion Williams is remembered to have spoken of his poisoned daggers in a boastful vein. He said to a friend in a I semi-jocose vet menacing way, " If you touch that you , are finished,'" but little heed was paid to his utterance, as it was thought he was inclined to show off before the I girls, of whose society he was greatly enamoured. There are not a few who begin to ask how Williams became possessed oY the means of which he made such cstentatious display, and tney venture to conjecture that he may be a thief and burglar as well as a murderer.

THE VICTIMS IDENTIFIED. The police at Rainhill have made an important dis- covery. The murdered woman's name is Marie Deeming. She was employed as a saleswoman in a fishmonger's shop in Liverpool kept by Messrs. Muirhead. The man who called himself Williams made her acquaintance, courted her, and subsequently married her. The mar- riage took place in Liverpool, Williams giving his name as Deeming, and described himself as a mining engineer. After the marriage he went to Hell, where he was appre- hended on a charge of forgery, and was imprisoned for twelve months. For some time afterwards he did not live with his wife, and in the meantime lie married another young woman in Hull. He wanted this young woman to go abroad with him, but she would not. He then rejoined his former wife, and lived with her at Birkenhead. They subsequently went to Capetown, where the child was born. They then returned to Bir- kenhead, and Deeming for a while disappeared. He has three brothers at present living at Birkenhead. The names of the children are Bertha, Marie, Lilla, and Sydney. Two of the sisters of the deceased woman pro- ceeded to Rainhill on Thursday afternoon for the purpose of identifying the victims. Mr Deeming, residing at Priory-road, Birkenhead, arrived at Rainhill on Thursday afternoon, and identi- fied the woman as his brother's wife and the children as his brother's.

THE OLD GARDENER AND THE CHILDREN. The old gardener who was interviewed on Wednesday stated that he saw two children in the yard of Din- ham Villa on the Saturday after Bank Holiday, made an important discovery on Thursday. He states that the last strawberries picked in his garden were boiled for preserves on Wednesday, July 28. This date is on the corners of the jars containing the jam. It was on the Saturday before this day that the two children purchased from him sixperinyworth of strawberries. On the Sun- day he saw a woman attired in a white dress cross the yard from the back door to the stable house, but did not see her return. On the Monday he heard children screaming inside the house,and it is surmised that this was the last heard of the parties. On the Saturday fallowing he heard the voice of a man and woman speak- ing. in the house, and this caused him to remark, after the -silence from Saturday to Monday, that they had evidently taken the house for week-ends. He was con- firmed in this belief by seeing that padlocks were put on the gate from a Monday to Wednesday. The nursery- man has seen the body of the woman, and he recognises her as the woman he had seen crossing the garden.

LATEST FROM AUSTRALIA. Aldelbourne telegram, dated Wednesday, says :—The police have been investigating the antecedents of Wil- liams,who is charged with murder. They have traced his career for a number of years past, and it appears he has been concerned in a variety of swindling transactions in Sydney, Melbourne, Cape Town, and England. They discovered that he passed under the aliases of Leeming, Swanson, and Lawson. Under the name of Lawson he was married to a Miss Matheson, at Beverley, Yorkshire in 1890. This lady he suddenly deserted. All attempts to trace the whereabouts of his reputed wife and child- ren, who mysteriously disappeared in Sydney, have proved fruitless, despite the exhaustive inquiries insti- tuted by the police.

div.head: COAL CRISIS.
div.p: THE COAL CRISIS.
WORKS STOPPED, AND TRADE DISLOCATED:

The crisis in the coal trade became an accomplished fact, on Saturday, the miners turning out in Lanca- hire, and Cheshire, North Wales, the Midlands and Somersetshire, Yorkshire, Staffordshire, and -Durham. The West Hartlepool shipbuilders and engineers are ar- ranging for supplies of coal from Northumberland and Scotland.

--- --- There was a slight disturbance at Castle Eden colliery on Tuesday night. The police interfered and ultimately dispersed the crowd. I number of vessels from southern ports arrived at West Hartlepool on Wednesday for coal, but were unable to obtain cargoes. A Newcastle telegram states that so great is the effect of the strike that on Wednesday two of the works of the United Alkali Company at Hebburn and East Jarrow were shut down owing to the lack of coal. This will lessen the production of bleaching powder and soda cry- stals, and will throw a large number of workmen out of employment on the Tyne. The Northumberland minets are making a move for an advance of wages to the extent of 25 per cent. CONFERENCE OF MINERS' DELEGATES.

The adjourned Conference of Miners'Delegates was open- ed in London on Wednesday, when it was reported that nearly 313,000 men had come out in accordance with the resolution of the Manchester meeting. Nothing was resolved upon as to the duration of the stoppage. The Conference will not come to a decision on this matter until to-day, but there are some grounds for anticipat- ing, a resolution to resume work next week. Mr. Woods, the president of the Conference, in a statement made to a reporter yesterday afternoon said that a week's stop- page would, he thought, be sufficient to achieve the oVject of the miners, and, so far as he could judge, that would be the decision of the meeting to-day. Mr. Woods further expressed himself in favour of a restric- tion of output by the adoption of a five-day working we. Prices on the_London Coal Exchange yesterday hados. tendency to fall. THE DECISLOI...—WORB TO Dr. RESUMED.

The Miners' Conference met again on Thursday morn- ing at ten o'clock, at the Westminster Palace Hotel, Mr. S. Weeds presiding. Ae, on previous occasions the pro- ceediAgs were private. The debate was a somewhat heated one, the chief paizt at issue being of course the duration of the stoppage. The Yorkshire delegates were in favcir of prolonging piay for another fortnight, but the Lancashire men prom,unced strongly on the side of those who recommended that work should be resumed on Monday. Eventually the arguments used by the Lancas- trian representatives prevalled, and the following resolu- tion was adopted practicaly unanimously :—" That seeing that the object for wkich the pits were stopped has been ackieved,this Conference advises all the miners

div.head: ..„eftv,,A
div.p: ..„eftv,,A
Iconnected with the Federation to resume work on 1 Monday."
THE SHIP CANAL.

More than 150,000 tons of coal are required per annum in the construction of the Manchester Ship Canal. Any failure in coal supplies would be a serious matter for the undertaking, the standing charges upon which are at least £l,OOO per day. Welearn that since the meeting of the miners' delegates in Manchester, when it was decided to recommend a cessation from work, the direc- tors of the Ship Canal Company have succeeded in putt- ing down a sufficient stock of coal to meet their require- ments during the remainder of March. The supplies have been obtained mainly from South Yorkshire and North Wales, which accentuates the fact that these colliery districts, as well as those of North Staffordshire and South Lancashire, will, upon the completion of the Ship Canal, have a nearer port for shipment into large steamers than any now existing. NORTHWICH AND DISTRICT. In Northwich, Winsford, Middlewich, and district the general opinion is expressed that the colliers' " holiday " will soon be over. Should the stoppage continue any length of time, the effects will certainly be disastrous, as so many depend on both salt and alkali manufactures. House coals have risen in price from 10d. _to is. and Is. id., but the supply seems fairly good. Notice has been given to the employes at;the Cheshire Alkali Company's works, Middlewich, that if a sufficient supply of coal is not obtainable, they will be compelled to suspend the men who work in the departments where fuel is requisite. At all the works under the Salt Union, the following notice has been issued—" We hereby give notice that should we not receive sufficient fuel for our require- ments your engagement with us will terminate from that time." At the Winsford offices of the Union, our repre- sentative was informed that they were not at all anxious as to the coal supply, and they did not intend to pay current prices. 3,000 MEN IDLE AT WARRINGTON. It is computel that something like 3,000 men have been idle this week in Warrington in consequence of the stoppage of works by the miners, and throughout tho , week the streets of the town have presented an unusually crowded appearance, owing to the number of unem- ployed men that were to be seen. The Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co., Limited, the largest em- ployers of labour in the town, temporarily suspended over 1,000 men on Monday morning, at the same time, however, retaining a sufficient number to deal with pressing contracts. At the works of the Whitecross Co., and those of Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Co., most of the workmen have also been temporarily thrown out of work. At Cockhedge Mills and at Messrs. Rylands Brothers' works there has, as yet, been no stoppage, there being in hand a sufficient stock of coal to meet requirements, unless the crisis be prolonged an unexpected length of time. The same remarks apply to the works of Mr. W. D. Houghton, at Sankey Bridges. The consumption of coal at Dallam and Bewsev forges,amounts, on the aver- age, to from 3,000 to 4,000 tons per week. The firm have done the best they could under the circumstances, and, although only two mills have been kept on, a large number of men are still employed in the engineering de- partments, and in the fitting and other shops. At one or two places there has been a slight reduction in the price charged for coal for household consumption, that of an inferior quality being sold at 103. per cwt., and the best at Ild, per cwt. The coal crisis has not affected the train service on the Cheshire Lines Railway, at any rate between Liver- pool and Manchester • but on the northern section of the London and North-Western Railway, which extends from Crewe to Carlisle, 300 coal trains have stopped running.

HAYDOCK. Sze. On Saturday the whole of the miners employed in the pits owned by Messrs. R. Evans and Co., Haydock, brought up their tools, in accordance with the resolution arrived at by the Miners' Federation. Nearly 3,000 men are affected by the stoppage, but a good number of surface men and day wag,emen are engaged in and about the pits, though no coal is brought up. The day wagemen are employed for the purpose of keeping the roads in the pits in repair, and seeing to any defects which may arise 1 in the roof. There have been several falls of roof in some of the pits, but nothing of a serious nature. Messrs. Evans and Co. are now loading from stock, but they are sadly inconvenienced in consequence of the L. and N. W. Rly. Co., having discontinued the running of several of their ordinary mineral trains. The firm naturally com- plain of the hindrance caused to their working, and allege that had the Railway Company maintained the usual complement of trains, they would have been enabled to get away a much larger supply of coal than under present circumstances. The various large works in the district have so far suffered no inconvenience in consequence of the stoppage, as when the first intima- tion of the cessation of work by the colliers was received, they at once laid in large supplies, and are thus provided against any contingency. GOLBORNE.

The colliers' " play-week "commenced on Monday, and it being the first play day, large crowds of men, hoth colliers and mill hands congregated in the principal thoroughfares, and discussed the situation. The Gol- borne Mills Company closed, at noon on Saturaay, their extensive cotton-spinning mills and weaving sheds, they having taken this step rather than pay the " fancy" price for coal to which, under their contract, they are -subject when the miners cease work. About 1,000 hands, all of whom are at present temporiarily stopped, are em- ployed at these mills. ST. HELENS.

The whole of the 3,500 colliers in the St. Helens dis- trict ceased work on Saturday, in accordance with the recommendation of the Miners' Federation. At some of the pits the week's "holiday " really started on the Friday night, but the arrangements for the stoppage fixed Saturday for the general cessation. Within the limits of the St. Helens district, as established by the Miners' Permanent Relief Society, there are five colliery firms—namely, Messrs. Pilkington Bros., whose collieries are known as" St. Helens" and" Ravenhead ;" Messrs. Bromilow, Foster, and Co., " Ashton's Green ;" the Whitecross Collieries Company, " Sherdley "and Peas- ley Cross ;" the Collins Green Collieries Company "Col- lins (treen" and "Bold," and Messrs. Glover and Co., " Phdinix." According to the last published report (1891.) of the same authority on the number of men em- ployed in and about the mines Messrs. Pilkington Brothers have found work for I,lsl:men ; Messrs. Bromi- low, Foster, and Co., 687; White Cross Company, 872; Collins Green Co. 922, and Messrs. Glover and Co. 244. These figures make a total of 3,876 persons working about the St. Helens coalfield., and on Saturday the whole of the operations were stopped for a week's "play." In- quiries elicited that at every pit the great majority of the colliers left their picks, spades, and other tools down the shafts, and the men came up from the workings under just the ordinary circumstances. In no case was there the slightest demonstration, and so far as the ap- pearance and conduct of the men were concerned they did not manifest any sign of ill-feeling, uneasiness, or panic. Conversations with seme of the more intelligent miners on Saturday afternoonand evening convinced one that, as a class, they regarded the prospective week's play with little concern or as a matter of no importance. They spoke hopefully and cheerfully as to the ultimate result of their combined action, and there was a remark- able readiness expressed to abide by the decision of their accredited leaders and delegates, whatever that decision might be.

The cessation of work by the colliers had a disastrous effect on other branches of industry in the town and dis- trict. It has previously been stated that the extensive 'works of the Loudon and Manchester Plate-glass Com- pany at Sutton and Ravenhead, where about 1,500 hands have been employed, were partially closed on Thursday, owing to the scarcity of fuel at ordinary prices, and notices that it might be necessary to cease working were posted by the United Alkali Company at their numer- ous chemical works in St. Helens, this notice affecting some thousands of men. The two large glassbottle making firms of Messrs. Cannington, Shaw, and Co., and Messrs. Nuttall and Co., are running their estab- ishments on half-time, and these facts, coupled with the recent stoppage of 600 men at Pocket Nook Glass- works, pending the completion of the alterations now in progress, have naturally caused some uneasiness among the tradespeople and residents of the town generally: The stoppage of the colliers to some extent intensified the unpleasant feelings regarding the future of the staple industries of the town entertained in some quar- ters. Mr. Thomas Glover, miners' agent, St. Helens, was the district delegate to the conference of Lancashire and Cheshire miners' representatives at Manchester on Saturday, and one of the Lancashire representatives at the national conference in London on Wednesday and Thursday this week. In conversation with a Press representative Mr. Glover stated that if the miners of the country had not decided to take the question affect- ing over-production into their own hands, nothing could I have prevented a general reduction of wages all round. By the stoppage they hoped to lessen the stocks the mas- ters had on hand,and maintain the present scale of wages under which colliers were paid. He roughly estimated that the total quantity of soal brought up to the shafts 4 the collieries in the St. Helens district averaged about 20,000 tons per week. Asked how the present rate of wages, compared with the wages paid a few years ago, Mr. Glover said there had been an increase of 40 per cent, during the last four or five years. He maintained that the higher prices charged for coal,and the increased consumption of coal during that period, had more than 3u,tshf justified the increase in the wages of the men. In the 15 years from 1873 to 1887 tha average s yearly 1405u,62t coal from the collieries of the kingdom wa tons ; in 1888 the output was 189,935,219 tons ; in 1889, 176,916,724 tons; and in 1890, the last year for which returns had been issued, 182,614,288 tons. He was con- fident that the present action of the miners was the best course they could adopt under the circumstances by which they were surrounded.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY. MARCH 19, 1892.

A Tun. Coal-owners' Association have Gigantic published what may be styled a Imposition, history of the negotiations which have led up to the groat strike in the coal ' trade ; and it must be conceded that they make out a good case, either for relief in the way of an immediate aper cent, reduction in wages,or for the reference to arbitration of the whole question in dispute between masters and men. On the other hand the miners, while admitting that wages have been advanced during the past few years, contend that they are not, receiving more than a fair sum for their labour ; and they urge that coal-owners must look for relief in some other direction.. Those who are most familiar with the arduous life of the collier are disposed to sympathise with him ; and the general public would be content to look on and let employer and employed "Fight it out," as the phrase goes, without troubling themselves, much about the matter, if it were not that the coal crisis is paralysing so many other industries and com- pelling other workmen to remain idle. It is monstrous that the trade of the country should be thus dislocated for a matter-of 5.0 r 71 per cent. reduction in the miner's wage ; and people are beginning to ask themselves why relief should not be given by redeeming royalty rents rather than by reducing wages ? If there is one man who ought to be first considered it is he who,, taking pick and spade in hand, leads a "sun- less life in the unwholesome mine." The capita- list who risks his money should COMB next, and the landlord, who finds nothing and does nothing, should come last. But, as matters stand at pre- sent, the landlord insists upon his. pound of flesh whoever else may go short. He lets his surface soil, it may be, for agricultural purposes; and, then he steps in, like a black-mailer, for a share of what other people may take the trouble to find beneath the surface! It is estimated that, on coal alone, the ground landlords of this, country pocket £14000,000 annually, taking the average royalty at eightpence per ton. They obtain this, in addi- tion of course to ordinary rent,, and then there are way-leaves and :fines to be taken into account. Not one of these men can be said to have done as much as the lifting of a little fi ger in the way of producing the mineral, which was in prepara- tion for the use of mankind tens of thousands of years before. they were born. Why then should they be permitted to exact these impositions? We can unclexstand the State levying a tax for the benefit of every person in the State, but it is wrong ox the face of it for individuals to usurp that position. Whatever may be said about land, it is certain that minerals should belong to the' nation.

But the blackmailing is not, of course, confined to coal ;it extends to limestone, and iron ore, and seriously affects the price of iron. "An Iron- master" who has had to blow out his furnaces and pay oft his men in consequence of the strike, writ- ing to the "Daily News "says : "Some of your readers will understa.nd what a tax upon industry are these heavy royalty rents when I tell them how it touches me and my men. Myl furnace produces, 50,000 tons of pig iron per annum. The royalty rent paid to landlordism for iron ore, coal, and limestone to produce 50,000 tons pig iron is 6s. per ton, or £15,000 per annum, to landlordism, for this furnace in one year. The wages to all the men employed at the furnace is 3s. per ton, or £7,500 per annum. The men work hard for their money, and deserve every penny they get, but what does the landlord or mineral lord do for his money? The collier, at the risk of life and limb, goes forth into the bowels of the earth to get the coal. Then why call upon the colliers for a paltry 5 per cent, reduction in wages and stop all trade and industry to secure it I could understand a great strike against mineral lords for a reduction of the royalty rents." Yes, we can all understand a great strike against royalty rents and it must come. How does it

look when the case of this Ironm aster is put inr this way: 100 men have to work hard for 5Ck weeks and receive, at 30s. per week, £7,50° In wages during the year; while a few landlords who haven't done a stroke of work receive £ls,oo°' for what ? For permitting other workmen to got the minerals required in the production of the pig iron It is pretty much the same in other depart: ments of industry. It is stated that the landlords' royalty on the coal which carries a steamer across the Atlantic amounts to a larger sum, than is pa to captain arid crew. Can we wonder that, with increasing knowledge of such gigantic imposition, workmen of all classes are growin<g restive; and that miners, pointing to the landlords, in effect say—" Please to lessen his plunder before you touch our pay." We grant that it is much easier to point to the evil than to find a speedy remedy. But if attention is not directed to the evil, it is obvicon that no remedy will be forth- coming. The miners on strike are at least causing people to think about royalty rents; and they cannot think without perceivirr, that, while trade is being hampered, tho nation is being defrauded.

THE people of this part of the Faminc. : An Appeal. country cannot have any true con- ception of the extent and, of the horrors of the famine in Russia, or they 1"On hasten to render some help—however small. Russian Famine Fund" has been opened ill London; and something over R.2;000 hes' be' received ; but London is only a part of the coun- try ; a similar fund ought to, be opened in eve,ll part of the Kingdom. It will not do to disauss the matter with the thought that Russia is a fa" away country, and that there are duties to be done nearer home. It was not so with the •when Ireland was scourged by famine in 181' ci they recognised humanity's call upon thenlo subscribed a sum exceeding £2,500.
