div.p: LOCAL NEWS.
IDNNS COUNTY COURT.
His Honour Judge :Shand held a sitting of this emit yesterday. The cause list contained no cases of public interest. °
SUPT. A Tllit ItTOM AND EXPLOSIVES.
The Runcorn Bench of Magistrates on Monday, ap- pointed Supt. Atherton an inspector under the Explo- sives Act.
ELLESMERE-ST. LITERARY SOCIETY, RUNCORN.

At the last meeting of the members Mr. A. Bentley delivered a lecture on "Elocutionary Expression," and also cave several recitals in an admirle manner. Mr. T. D. Cullis presided. WIDNES PARISH CHURCH: Special services were held at the above church, on Sunday, in behalf of the Church Pastoral Aid Society, and two excellent sermons were preached by the Rev. R. F. Downhatn, M.A., of Liverpool. There were large congregations.

div.head: SEPARATION ORDER DISREGARDED.
div.p: A SEPARATION ORDER DISREGARDED.

George Holt, an engine driver, was brought before the Runcorn Bench, on Saturday, charged with failing to obey a maintenance order. The prisoner had been ordered to pay 153. a week towards his wife and family, and he was eight weeks in arrears.--The prisoner said the weekly sum was more than he could par, and he wished to have the question reconsidered. The Bench ordered him to pay the amount due or go to goal for a month and Mr. Handley advised him to pay the moniy to save himself further trouble. SCALDING FATALITY AT RUNCORN.

Mr. J. E. Worsley, thecoroner for the honour and fee of Halton, held an inquest at Runcorn en Monday, on the body of Thomas Herbert Whitfield, aged four years, son of John Whitfield, of 36 Lock-st., Runcorn. On the 16th February the deceased upset a kettle of boiling water, and the liquid was poured over his neck, back, and left side. He was terribly scalded, and although everything that medical skill could suggest was done for him he died from shock on the 11th inst. A verdict of" Accidental death "was returned. MISSION SERVICES AT HALTON.

A ten day; Mission, which has been held in Halton Parish Church, concluded on Tuesday evening. The services each day have been very largely attended, in spite of the inclement weather. The four addresses to men working at Mr. Reynolds's tannery, Astmore, havp been listened to with attention by nemiy the whole staff of workmen, and a very large congreg,ntion assembled in church on Sunday atterrpoon, for the men's service at three o'clock, many being present who had not been in a place of worship for years. At the evening service on Sunday, both tha church and the mission-room were crowded. The missioner is the Rev. .1. P. Ashing, of the Church Parochial Mission Society, assisted by the Rev. A.. P. Reynolds, vicar of Kingsley.

div.head: THRFT FROM A BOAT AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THRFT FROM A BOAT AT RUNCORN.

On Saturday at the Runcorn Police- Court, before Messrs. James 'Handley and G. L. Davies, a youth named Samuel Thninins, of 37, Potter-street, Brierley 11111, Staffordshire, was charged with stealing one cap, one coat, one hankerchief, one pair of boots, and four plates, value 95., the goods of George Jones, captain of the boat Esther. The prisoner had been on the vessel about a week. At noon en Friday the captain went on shore, and on returning an hour later, found Timmins had taken his departure. The articles in question were also missing. P.C. Fryer apprehended the prisoner in Northwich-road, Sutton, the same afternoon, with the goods in his posses- sion. Ile acknowledged the theft, and was fined 10s., or in default seven days' imprisonment.

div.head: MURDEROUS ASSAULT AT WIDNES.
div.p: MURDEROUS ASSAULT AT WIDNES.

Before Mr. 11. ‘Vacl:-. Deacon at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, George Brassington, Marsh-st., was charged with doing grievous bodily harm to Michael Redmond, Marsh-st.—Patrick Redmond, Marsh-st., said the defen- dant and his orother Michael were quarrelling on Satur- day night, when prisoner picked UD the " jockey bar' from the hearth and struck his brother on the head with it. The blow rendered him insensible.—Dr. Hutchinson said the injured man was suffering from a wound in the temple about two inches in length and penetrating to the bone, also a contused wound half-an-inch long. In addition to these, there was a wound on the eye level, completely detaching it from the ball of the eye. He was in a very serious condition, and unable to appear.— P.C. Evans proved apprehending the prisoner, who said " I plead guilty to striking him with my fist, but not with the bar."—Prisoner was remanded until Thursday. The prisoner was again brought before the Bench on Thursday and committed for trial.

div.head: FUNERAL OF AN OLD RIINCORNIAN._
div.p: FUNERAL OF AN OLD RIINCORNIAN._

The remains of Mr. William Bradbury, of 25, Bridge- street, Runcorn, aged 94 years, were interred in the Nonconformist portion of the Cemetery, on Sunday. The cortege consisted of a hearse and four coaches, and the mourners were Mr. and Mrs. Thomason (daughter), Mr. and Mrs. Brimelow (daughter), Mr. William Hardley (great grandson), Mr. John Bradbury (grandson), and his wife, Mary Hardley (granddaughter), Joseph Brittle- low (grandson), Mr. and Mrs. William Carroll (erand- daughter), Mr. Arthur Hardley (great-grandson), Mr. W. B. Brimelow (grandson) and wife, Mr. Samuel Brimelow (grandson), Miss Mary J. Bradbury (granddaughter), Mrs. Price (niece), Miss Southworth (niece),and Mrs. Moyle (neice). The officiating minister was the. Rev. W. Arrowsmith. The mourning coaches were supplied by Henry Jackson, of Bridge-st. A brief sketch of the life of the deceased veteran appeared in the last issue of this journal. ALLEGED BURGLARY 13Y AN ACTOR AT WIDNES.

Yesterday, at the Widnes Police Court, a man who gave his name as William Pritchard, was charged with burglariously breaking and entering the booking office at the station of the Midland Railway, Whines, between half-past ten on Saturday night and eight o'clock on Sunday morning, and stealing therefrom moneys, keys, and clothing, valued altogether at ER. Three automatic machines on the station platform had been tampered with. Suspicion against the prisoner was aroused, as he was seen near the station about midnight on Satur- day. Police-constable Worsfold visited his lodgings, 3, Viaduct-street, at noon on Sunday, and found prisoner in bed. The clothes and keys were found by the const- able under the bed prisoner was sleeping on. When charged with the offence, prisoner said, " I have done it. I can't realise that I did it ; but it's done." He was remanded for a week. Prisoner is said to be a discharged soldier, and during the previous week had been acting with the Whipping Post Company at Alexandra Theatre, Widnes.

div.head: ATTEMPTED SUICIDE NEAR _WIDNES.
div.p: ATTEMPTED SUICIDE NEAR _WIDNES.

Thomas Rigby, 8, Moss-street, Widnes, was brought before Mr. Deacon at Widnes Police Court, on Saturday, charged with attempting to commit suicide by drown- ing, in a pit near Bold, on the previous evening.—Wini- fred Collier, defendant's step daughter, said she was a servant at the Horns Inn, Farnworth. Her father came to see her, on Friday afternoon, and had two pints of beer and his tea. When he left the Horns Inn, about 7-30 p.m., he said, "Good night, Winnie, you will not I see me again." She followed him down the lane, and saw him jump into a pit on the side of the road.—J. Far- rel, Warrington, said he dragged the defendant out of the pit. His head and shoulders were in the water, but his feet were on the side. When he was taken out he said he would never be happy until he had "gone stiff." —Defendant, in reply to his Worship, said he was very low-spirited at the time, and had pains in his head. Be felt better that morning, and he had work to go to at Fiddler's Ferry, on Monday.—Mr. Timmis (to defen- dant's wife) : Have you any money ?—Mrs. Rigby • No. and I have ;three little children to keep.--Mr. Timmis: Will you go to the Workhouse hospital ?—Defendant: I want to go to work.—Mr. Timmis ; You are not fit to work yet, and I want to act kindly towards you. Yon will be better there for a short time.—Defendant said he was willing to go.—He was then handed over to the re- lieving officer.

div.head: Fr it! TT
div.p: Fr it! TT
THE EXAMINER, SATL RDA Y, MARCH 19, 1892.
WIDNES CYCLE CLUB.
The members of this club held the first parade of the season on Thursday evening, and attracted much attention.
SCENES IN CHINA, In Lacey-st., Schools, Widnes, on Thursday evening, Mr. J. Robinson delivered a lecture on the above sub- ject illustrated by limelight views.
BRUNSWICK MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.
At the weekly meeting on Wednesday, the Rev. Wm. Arrowsmith delivered a lecture on "John Wesley," to a large audience. Mr. Simister presided.
UXIVERSITY_ EXTENSION LECTURES AT RUNCORN.

The sixth and last of the series of lectures on the His- tory of Florence, by the Rev. W. Hudson Shaw will be delivered on Monday evening in Bethesda School. The subject is" Fall of the Republic and Michael Angelo."
ELECTION OF GUARDIANS IN RUNCORN UNION.

Our readers are reminded that Saturday, March 26th, is the last day for receiving nominations for this election. The present members at Runcorn are the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. P. Speakman, C.C., S. Taylor, W. Lightburn,and T. Lea. LICENSING MATTERS AT WIDNES, At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday Mr. Geo. Atkin Forster was granted permission to sell at the Central Hotel, under the licence held by Mr. Parke ; and Mrs. Lewis, of the Bridge Hotel, was granted permission to sell in place of her husband, deceased.

div.head: MILL BROW BRASS BAND, RUNCORN.
div.p: MILL BROW BRASS BAND, RUNCORN.

In aid of this band the Rev. J. Hanby gave a lecture on" A trip to London," in Mill Brow Wesleyan School, on Monday evening. Limelight views were shown by Mr. F. Pope. A musical programme was gone through by the band, and several local vocalists.

div.head: RUNCORN FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY.
div.p: RUNCORN FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY.

At the monthly meeting of this committee, on Wed- nesday, Mr. W. Handley presiding, the librarian re- ported that during the past month 1,904 vols, had been issued, an increase of 19. In the reference department 37 vols. had been issued, increase 6. THE SEAMIN'S INSTITUTE, RUNCORN.

In connection with this Institute it has been decided to issue cards of membership, so that those who wished could pay a small contribution towards the expenses of the place. The cards will'also be of use to sailors when in other places where similar institutions are in existeuce.
WIDNES AND DISTRICT TIIADES COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of the above was held on Mon- day night, when it was decided to have the resolution of December 14th printed and sent to every member of the Local Boards of Widnes and Runcorn, to elicit their private opinion thereon, and, if necessary, to publish the same for the information of the Trades Unions of the district. A unanimous vote of thanks was accorded to Messrs. Tilley and Beech, and the secretary was instructed to write to them stating their appreciation of the sensible remarks made at the late Board meeting at Widnes, with regard to the making of Lowerhouse-lane. A hope was expressed .that they will not let the matter rest there.
WESTON BIBLE AND MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS. -

The usual weekly meeting of this class was held on Monday night last in the Wesleyan schoolroom, under the presidency of Mr. James Ford, when a paper was read by Mr. H. Johnson, on the" Life and Writings of St. Paul." _ .
UMBRELLAS riF.COVERED.-J. and W. DuTTox, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. THE TUNNEL AT FIDDER'S FERRY.

Signal progress was made last week in the boring operations at Fidler's Ferry, and up to Saturday a total for the week of something like 56ft. or 57ft. had been completed. Considering the nature of the strata now being dealt with, this is considered very satisfactory. SAFETY BICYCLES.—J. S. Garland. 51. Bridge-st., War- rington. See advertisement on page 4.

div.head: PRINCESS-ST. SUNDAY_ SCHOOL. WIDNES.
div.p: PRINCESS-ST. SUNDAY_ SCHOOL. WIDNES.

The annual distribution of prizes to Sunday school scholars for regular and punctual attendance was held on Thursday evening, and there was a crowded audience. Miss Peters, of Bold, presented the prizes, and a miscel- laneous programme of music, &c., was gone through. Mr. W. liodglcinson presided.

div.head: UNIONIST MEETING _AT RUNCORN.
div.p: UNIONIST MEETING _AT RUNCORN.

The electors of Runcorn will have the opportunity of listening to the Unionist candidate for the division on Tuesday evening next, when a public meeting is to be held in the Public Hall. Mr. John Brundrit, J.P.' will preside, and the principal speakers will be Lord Cran- borne, M.P., and Mr. George Whiteley. the candidate. WRST.EYAN HOMII MISSIONS, RUNCORN. '"

In aid of these missions special sermons will be preached la St. Paul's Chapel on Sunday, by the Rev. S. F. Collier, a local gentleman who has achieved fame- as a missionary in Manchester. On Monday evening a public meeting will be held, and addresses will be de- livered by Mr. Collier and 'the, Rev. S. Chadwick, of Leeds.

div.head: Sr. PATRICK'S DAY AT WIDNES.
div.p: Sr. PATRICK'S DAY AT WIDNES.

This Saint day was celebrated in the usual manner on Thursday. In the evening a concert was held in the Drill Hall, in aid of St. Mary's Catholic School, and there was a large audience. A musical programme was gone through by Mrs. Doyle, Miss Dwyer, Messrs, J. B. Sim chair, T. J. Hayes, C. Parsonage, and G. Connolley. A buporpus Irish sketch was also given.
_ ACE-BRAND SPADES.—J. S. GARLAND, Ironmonger, Bridge-st., Warrington. WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.

The Ratepayers' Association have decided to nominate four candidates at the forthcoming election,and a contest seems unavoidable. The gentlemen proposed are Messrs. H. Singleton, Tom Smith, Toni (Dr.) Gerrard, and James Carroll. It is also probable that the Irish National League will nominate several candidates, and the name of Mr. John Williamson is mentioned. Wed- nesday next is the last day for nominations. • A SUCCESSFUL MBSION AT HALTON CHURCH. A large congregation assembled in Halton Church on Tuesday evening, to take part in the thanksgiving ser- vice, which was held for the blessings Nceived during the ten days' mission. An impressive sermon was preached by the missioner, the Rev. J. P. Cushing, of the Church Parochial Mission Society. A striking testimony to the success of the mission are the offerings, which total, £29 Is. 6d. The largest offering was half A sovereign.

div.head: ST. PATRICK'S DAY AT RUNCORN.
div.p: ST. PATRICK'S DAY AT RUNCORN.

The natives of the Emerald Isle were "wearing o' the green" on Thursday in celebration of their patron saint. In the morning mass, followed by the benediction, was celebrated at St. Edwards' Church, and the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi delivered an appropriate address. In the even- ing the children of the school performed the operetta "Dick Whittington," and gave drill and action songs. The mistresses,Miss Cowerford and Miss Dague,are to be congratulated upon the effective training of the children. UNIISRELLAS IigCOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-et., Wa:ri ngtt i.—Advt. RUNCORN TOWN BAND.

The members of this band are making an earnest effort to obtain a complete set of first-class electro- plated instruments, and towards the £lOO required as a deposit towards the cost, the sum of £6O has been ob- tained by subscription. While grateful for this valuable aid, much more is yet required, and a prize drawing is being held in order to still further increase the fund. On Monday next a ball will be held with the same aim in view, and tho band ask for the support of their patrons, as they are wishful to have the instruments for the Whitsuntide festivities. WANTON WINDOW SMASHING AT WIDNES.

On Wednesdetv, at Widnes Police Court, before Mr. H. Wade Deacon, Mary Jane Riley and Catherine Hynes, well-known characters, were charged with doing wiltul damage to the amount of £7 us. 61 to a plate glass window of the Waterloo Vaults, the property of Peter Walker and Soas, Ltd. They were also charged with doing wilful damage, to the amount of £5 3s. Bd., to a plate glass window of the White Star Inn, Queen-st., the property of John Gerrard. The prisoners at midnight on the previous night appeared to have broken the windows out of mere wantonness. They were com- mitted for trial at the Quarter Sessions. BASSINETTES. Garland, Ironmonger, Warrington and • Rarlestown. WIDNES WESLEYAN METHODIST CIRCUIT.

The quarterly meeting was held in Lacy-st. school, on Monday. The stewards presented the quarterly state- ment of accounts, which was very satisfactory, and the numerical statement made by the Chairman (the Rev. W. Pritchard) showed the circuit was in the same posi- tion as last year. Mr. Pritchard accepted an invitation to remain in the circuit another year; and the meeting approved of a provincial invitation which had been given the Rev. Stevenson, of Stockton-on-Tees, to succeed Mr. Meek, who leaves at the next Conference. Mr. T. A. Brady was recommended as a candidate for the ministry, and Mr. T. Ormroyde was elected as a delegate to the distri it meeting in May. MAGIC LANTERN ENTERTAINMENT AT RUNCORN BOARD
Scnoot.

The combination of amusement with instruction is being carried out at Greenway-road Board School with excellent results, both as regards the attendance of scholars, and in arousing in the pupils an interest in their work. Frequent entertainments have been given during the winter season, and the subjects illustrated and des- cribed have been of a varied character. On Thursday evening the geography of India, which is part of the Evening School Syllabus, was shown to the students in a series of excellent magic lantern views, and Mr. Epps acted the part of guide admirably. The entertainment vvas repeated to the day-school children last evecang,who were in addition made merry by illustrations of the comical story of " The Lazy Traveller and one of the Dagonet Ballads. The oxy-hydrogen lantern was inam- pulated by Mr. Bowyer and Mr. Rosser.

div.head: LECTURE ON ENGINEERING AT RUNCORN.
div.p: LECTURE ON ENGINEERING AT RUNCORN.

Under the auspices of the Science and Art Committee, Mr. W. J. Yarwood, mechanical engineer to the River Weaver Trustees, Northwich, delivered a lecture on en- gineering. The subject was "benefits derived from com- pounding at pressures varying from 40 to 120Ibs. to the square inch," and it was illustrated by full working drawings of engines, and also indicating cards were ex- hibited by the oxy-hydrogen light. Mr. Yarwood dealt with the subject in a comprehensive and practical man- ner, and he held the attention of his large audience to the close of his lecture. At the conclusion a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the lecturer, on the motion of Mr. W. Timmins, seconded by Mr. Robert Rawlinson, and supported by Captain Le Couteur. A similar compliment was paid to the Chairman, on the motion of Mr. Yarwood,seconded by Mr. E. W. Humph- reys, who drew attention to the valuable service Mr. Wiswall had rendered, and he hoped would continue to render to technical education in the town.

div.head: PRESENTATION TO DR. O'KEEFFE AT WIDNES.
div.p: PRESENTATION TO DR. O'KEEFFE AT WIDNES.

In recognition of the valuable services rendered by Dr. O'Keeffe to the town, a number of ratepayers waited upon that gentleman on Monday evening at his resi- dence, and presented him with an illuminated address, and a cheque for a substantial amount. IMajor Wareing, in making the presentation, said the doctor was first elected a member of the Local Board in 1880, and he had served on several important committees from that time until 1891,when he retired to become the medical officer. For a number of years he was a guardian of the town- ship, and was at present a member of the School Board, on which he had held a seat since 1877. He was now chairman of the Technical Instruction Committee, and, taken altogether, Dr. O'Keeffe had a public record that any man might be proud of, And the presentation that evening was not from any local, political, or religious body, but had been subscribed for by men of all shades of opinion.—Mr. D. Wright and Mr. F. Heyes also bore testimony to Dr. O'Keeffe's services to the town, and Dr. O'Keeffe having suitably:tacknowledged the gifts, the proceedings terminated.

div.head: TECHNICAL SCHOOL FOR ALTRINCHAM.
div.p: A TECHNICAL SCHOOL FOR ALTRINCHAM.

The Altrincham Local Board haying acquired possession of the Literary Institute, a building worth about £4,000, are desirous of enlarging it, so as to establish a Technical School. They hare ap- plied to the County Council for a grant towards the building fund. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.-7. and W. DUTTON', Sankey-t., Warringtou.—Adet. THE MUSIC HALL QUESTEY:I.

At the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, Mr. Mulholland, barrister, instructed by Mr. J. P. Mearns, applied on behalf of Mr. Charles Liptrott, of the Salisbury Hotel, for sanction to proposed alterations to the premises named, in order to pro- vide better accomrnedation in the concert room at- tached to the hotel. Chief-constable Wood strongly opposed the application. He said he considered the facilities for drinking would be increased, and as a matter of principle he was against music halls being connected with public houses. The bench retired, and on their return into court the chair- man stated that they had decided to refuse the ap- plication. UMURELLAS REOOVERED,—J. and W. DurToN, Sankey-st., Warrington.— Advt. A BOY DROWNED IN RUNCORN DOCKS. On Wednesday, Mr. IVorsley held an iiwuest at Runcorn Police Court, on the body of Jonathan Dickenson, a boy ten years of age, who was drowned in the ii'enton Dock on Monday evening.—Thomas Dickenson, of Marsden Green, near Manchester, fiatman, father of the deceased, said his flat was moored alongside a schooner. About half-past five deceased left the cabin, and ten minutes later he found ins cap in the small boat of the schooner. He at once obtained a pair of grappling irons and brought! the body up the first throw. Ho was quite dead. The deceased had been accustomed to go out into small boats: he could not keep him out.—Joseph Taylor, flatman, corroborated.—P.C. Crowder said from the way the body was found, he thought the boy had been under the schooner and so prevented from rising or shouting for help.—A verdict of "accidentally drowned" was returned. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED,—J. and W. DUTTON, Satikey- it. Warrington.— Advt.

CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT WINNVICK. The annual meeting of the Conservatives of Win- wick was held in the Schoolroom, Wiuwick, on Tuesday night. Tnere was only a moderate attend- ance. Mr. Cooper presided. A letter of apology for inability to attend was read from Mr. G. Comber, Rowley-brow, Knutsford, the chairman of the local association. On the proposition of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. Mather, Mr. Comber was re-elected chairman of the association. Mr. R. Owen was re- elected vice-chairman. Mr. Cooper was re-elected secretary and treasurer. Messrs. J. Swinton and P. Longton were re-elected delegates to the Council. Mr. W. Carson moved the adoption of a resolution, expressing the unabated confidence of the meeting in the Unionist Government, and tendering their thanks to Mr. T. NV. Legh for his able representation of the Newton division. Mr. Clarke seconded the motion, which was supported by Mr. J. Fielding in a lengthy speech. and adopted. UMBRELLL9 RECOVERED,—J . and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: WIDNES SCtIOOL BOARD. .
div.p: WIDNES SCtIOOL BOARD. .

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday. Mr.T. S. Tirnmis presided, and there were present the Rev. Dean Finegan, Rev. Father Clarke, Major Wareing, Dr. McDonnell, Messrs. B. Brown, S. Quinn, G. H. Danby (clerk).

div.head: REMISSION OF YENS AND REGULAR ATTENDANCE.
div.p: REMISSION OF YENS AND REGULAR ATTENDANCE.

The District Education Committee reported that dur- ing February there were 389 persons summoned before the Committee for contravention of the Education Act; nine were prosecuted and convicted. There were three applications for the payment of school fees which were recommended to be paid.—A discussion arose as to the cause of so many breaches of the Education Act, and the Chairman said some parents were " crossedly " obdur- ate and would not send the children to school. • They came to the Police Court and were fined again and again but still there was no improvement in the attendance. Some people had paid pounds and pounds in fines.— Major Wareing : Fern or no fee they don't send their children to school.—Mr. Deacon atid as far as he could see ths remission of fees had not improved the attend- ance.—Dean Finegan said it was important that the schools should have regular attendance because th grant depended on it. It was not altogether a question of school fees ; the severe weather they were having might have something to do with it.—Mr. Deacon said there was a great deal of sickness about, and from information he had from the Secretary of one of the Clubs, there was absolutely more sickness this year than there was last year, which was a remarkable thing. For acme time there had been much sickness amongst children, and whenever this was pleaded the Cammittee had to accept it as a good reason for non-attendance.—Dean Finegan said the Guardians had made arrangements to pay for medical certificates in cases of poverty. Mr. Deacon expressed his pleasure at this step and said it would help the Committee in their work. The discussion then ceased.

div.head: TEACHING OF PUPIL TEACHERS.
div.p: THE TEACHING OF PUPIL TEACHERS.

The School Management Committee submitted a scheme for placing the instruction of the pupil teachers under the control of a teacher set apart for the work, instead of being carried out sections as at present ; and they recommended that Miss Clayden be appointed instruc- tress of the central classes for female pupil teachers at a salary of £ll3 per annum,rising according to the scale of the Board for senior girls':mistresses, with an average attendance 01 200 or more, together with a bonus of 103. for each pupil teacher (or candidate, if subsequently apprenticed in the Board's own service) who passed H.M. Inspector's examination, and obtained the mark good ; and 25 per cent, of the drawing grant earned by the pupil 'teachers and candidates.—Dean Finegan, in moving the adoption of the scheme, said it had been a source of regret that the instruction of pupil teachers had not shown better results; but the committee hoped for an improvement under this scheme.—After a brief discussion, the scheme was unanimously approved.

FREEING THE UPPER STANDARDS. The School Management Committee made the follow- ing recommendations : That on and after March 21st, 1892, no School fees be charged for any child in Stand- ards V., VI., and VII., in any of the schools under the Board, until further notice, but that thoy shall be required to provide their own books and stationery, and that regulation 52 in the rules for the Government of Board Schools be amended accordingly.—Dean Finegan moved the acceptance af the recommendation, and said the object of the Committee was to see that the Board did not lose anvthing.—The Chairm in : The children to provide books and stationery.—Dean Fine- gan: They will now do something towards the mainten- ance of the school.—The Chairman : Are you not giving with one hand and taking it back with the other.—Dean Finegan said they were forced to give with one hand.— The Chairman said the children had now to pay a penny fee, and his information was that the cost of books, &c., would be more than a penny.—Dean Finegan said lie did not think it would : it would be almost nil but that did not effect the principal object the freeing of the standards. If they could keep tho penny they would keep it. (Laughter.)—The Chairman said he usually seconded all minutes to expedite business but he could not second that motion as it stood. • He should be glad if Dean Finegan would strike out the second part of the motion. The business of that Board was education and not to save tee rates, and that Board would be more efficient if they kept the children in the higher standards as long as they could. When children left school early much that they had learnt be- came lost, and if the Board could keep them at school longer it would be better for themselves, better for the parents and better for society generally.—Dean Finegan said the Committee wore unanimous on the point, and they did not think it judicious that a commercial educa- tion should be given free. With regard to the business of the Board being to educate, he agreed with him to a certain extent, but at the same time they ought to be as careful as they could .—Mr. Deacon said if they were going to knock off the fees let them do it thoroughly.— Dean Finegan said it was their duty to receive fees as far as they could receive them to the extent of 2s. 11d., they must adjust the income so as not to press upon chil- dren, but at the same time be no disadvantage to the

Board. The Chairman said he had taken the trouble to ask some of the teachers what books and stationery would cost, and the average was lid. a week,so that the Committee were giving id. and takinr, lid.back.—Dsan I Finegan said when it was increasing salaries he never got any opposition. He complained that this information had been obtained over the heads of the Committee, and he objected to it being sprung upon them in that way. If the recommendations were not passed he would resign the Committee.—The Chairman said he did not like to be put into that position—that the Dean said he would resign. He must please withdraw that.—Dean Finegan did so.—The Chairman said he considered it his duty RS a member of the Board to inform himself upon all matters brought before the Board, and he took it as a matter of course that the Committee would be in posse*. sion of the cost of books and stationery. He suggested that the recommendation should be taken back to Corn- mitt.e.—Dean Finegan said he would not take it back.— The Chairman pressed him to do so.—Dean Finegan: Do you ask me as a personal favour? We are not here as friends; we are here to conduct business and I would not like to do anything outside my official position as a member of tho Board.—Father Clarke seconded the motion.—The Chairman proposed an amendinest, that the portion referring to books and stationery be struck out.—Mr. Deacon seconded.—For the amendment there voted the Chairman, Mr. Deacon, and Mr. Brown. Against: Dean Finegan, Father Clarke, Dr. O'Keeffe, Dr. McDonnell, and Mr. Quinn.—Major Wareing said he would not vote until he had full information to vote upon.—The Chairman declared the motion carried.
FINANCY..
The Finance Committee reported receipts amounting to £35 9s. 9d., and reyonmended the payment of ac- counts amounting to £859 O. 81.
THE FEE GRANT.
The Clerk said he had received a letter from the E lu- cational Department enclosing cheque for £335, being the fee grant fur the past quarter.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT RUNCORN, &c.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORIESP3NDNINT.

Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss, M.P. for Widues Divi- sion, has been appointed private secretary to Mr. W. L. Jackson, Ml'., chief secretary for Ireland. In October of the present year the triennial election of members of Widnes School Board takes place. and the proceedings at a meeting of that body, on rues- day, ought to show the ratepayers who are their true friends, and working to further their real interests in the matter ot education. Dean Finegan acting on behalf of the School Management Com- mittee, proposed that the children in the upper standards of the Board schools should•be freed from the payment of school pence, but at the same time requiring the scholars in future to purchase their own books and stationary. The farce of this pro- posed freedom was at once disclosed by the chair- man, who described the committee as giving with one hand in order to take it back with the other, and disclosed information obtained from the teach- ers, which showed that while the school fee was only Id. per week, books and stationary would aver- age lid. per week. So that the supposed gift is really a profitable transaction. That the Chairman should have exercised his privilege as a member of the Board and gather in- formation outside the Committee, gave 'great um- brage to the Dean, who lost his temper at the cool logic of the figures and threatened to resign from the Committee if the recommendation were not passed. He declined to take back the minute for further consideration,and eventwilly it was adopted by five votes to three, Major Waring holding aloof because of the insufficient information. The names of those who voted for the motion are highly sug- gestive, as being those of the most pronouced ad- vocates of denominational education.

It is well to remember that when the Assisted Education Act was adopted by the Board,the penny fee was imposed out of consideration to the De- nominational Schools, the managers of which,it was stated,could not afford to make their schools wholly free. It would appear that this charge of a penny was not unlikely to cause a loss of.a portion of the fee grant from Government, and the Committee to get out of the difficulty have diverted it to another channel, by making the purchase of books and stationery a means of taxing the parents of the scholars. All who wish to see education valuable and beneficial, must agree with the chairman that scholars must be kept at school as long HS possible, and every inducement offered them to do so, but to free the lower standards and tax the higher is not the way to do this.

If the ratepayers are wise they will elect men to the Board who have only one single purpose—to make the schools the most efficient and successful of their class, and not send gentlemen who will sinwly hold a watching brief on behalf of denomin- ational schools, and whose object is to retard rather than to aid the progress of the ratepayers' schools. Managers of denominational schools can scarcely be expected to work for the success of the Board Schools with the determination and singleness of purpose of those who are in favour of free educa- tion, untrammelled by all denominational bias.

There is one thing the members of the Board School might set about remedying at once, and they would earn the gratitude of the members of the Press who have to record their proceedings. From some cause or other they have become accustomed to carry on their discussions in a low conversational tone, and it is with the utmost diffi- culty that the reporters can carry out their duties and give to the public an accurate digest of what takes place. lam sure t his has only to be mention- ed to be remedied, for even a slight raising of the voice would relieve the " professors of the winged art " of much anxiety and trouble.

A Fatal Idea! Such was the description by the Coroner at an inquest this week, of the impression of a boatman that he could not rescue a woman from the canal unless a policeman was present. From the evidence it appeared conclusive that the poor woman had been past all human aid some time when the man first saw her, as her face was in the water, but her body was buoyed up by her clothes. This is not the first instance in the locality of persons fearing to bring forth a body from the water until the formality of apprising a constable had been gone through, and I remember some years ago there were grave doubts entertained whether a life was not lost through a man failing to promptly bring to land what he considered a dead body. After the Coroner's explicit statement that it is the duty of any man who sees an apparently drowned person to at once bring the body to land and adopt reme- dies for resuscitation, it is to be hoped that the idea that a constable must be present to act as a kind of Master of Ceremonies will have a sudden death with no hops of a resurrectiou.

In response to a desire extensively expressed, the Committee of the Runcorn Liberal Club are arreing- inr.,, a social meeting for the purpose of recognising the signal service rendered by Mr. W. Ockleston to the Liberal party in the recent County Council contest in Runcorn North. A knife and fork tea will be the initial stage of the proceedings, and afterwards there will be brief speeches and fraternal greetings, and communion. Of course Mr. Ockles- ton will be the guest of the evening, and there will also be invited Dr. Hodgson, Mr. Geo. Cooke, Mr. W. R. Earp, Mr, J. F. L. Brunner, and our respected member, Mr. J. T. Brunner. Tuesday, the 29th met, has been fixed for the interesting gathering.

div.head: SAD END OF AN OLD WOMAN AT RUNCORN.
div.p: SAD END OF AN OLD WOMAN AT RUNCORN.
A FATAL IDEA.

On Monday, at the London and North-Western Hotel, Runcorn, Mr. J. E. Worsley, coroner, held an inquest on the body of Mary Ridman, a boatwoman, who was found drowned in the Bridgewater Canal, near Savages Bridge, on `c'aturday evening.—John Ridman said the 'deceased was his wife and 78 years of age. He left her on the boat at three o'clock on Saturday.—John Ridman, sen., said he saw his mother on the bank at four o'clock. Mis idea was that she had tripped over a rope into the water.— Thomas Withey. a boatman, said he saw the deceased floating between two boats about five o'clock. He held her head out of water for two minutes, bat did not lift the body out because he was under the impression that a policeman ought to be present. The woman was per- fectly dead when he first saw her.—P.C. Crowder said when he arrived on the scene, the body was on the bank and several members of the Ambulance Association were trying to restore animation. Life was, however, extinct and their efforts were of no avail. The place where de- ceased's boat was moored was approached by a narrow footpath sloping down to the water's edge, and it was slippery with ice and snow. It was difficult and danger- ous to walk along, and he got aboard a flat rather than attempt it. There was nothing to show whether deceased had slipped in or had fallen over a mooring rope.—The Coroner, in summing up, said it ought to be generally known that whenever a body was seen in the water it was the imperative duty of the person who saw it to im- mediately recover it and obtaining aid to at once attempt to restore animation. The idea that a body must remain in the water until a policeman could be got to see it

landed was a most fatal idea, anti ought to be contra- dicted as widely as possible. 1,-1 this case his own opinion was that the body was deak i when the witness saw it, but there might be other cast 's where animation might be restored by taking prompt m, ‘msures.—A verdict of "Accidentally drowned" was returt 'ed.—The Coroner asked Mr. Simister, who appeared for the Ship Canal Company whether that dangerous footpat`htould not be improved.—Mr. Simister said when the ant sw had cleared I away there would be very little slope, and h. did not see that anything could be done, as the place was' merely an accommodation for beats. However, he woula I lay the matter before his princjpals, and if anything a 'ould oe done it would be done.

div.head: _ WIDNES DIVISION CONSERVATI VP ASSOCIATION. SPEECH BY ME. MOSS, M.P.
div.p: _ WIDNES DIVISION CONSERVATI VP ASSOCIATION. SPEECH BY ME. MOSS, M.P.

On Wednesday evening a Conservative demon- stration under the auspices of the above associa- tion was hemd in Widnes Drill Hall, which had been made gay for the occasion by streamers stretching across the building from various points. There was a large audience, which included a number of ladies. Major Cross, chairman of the association, presided, and these on the platform were Mr. T. C. Edward Moss, ALP., Mr. T. B. Royden. M.P., Messrs IT. H. Hornby, A. Mackenzie, Smith, Richard Lewis, James White, A. S Mather, Joseph Matthews, R. B. Weison, J. B. Strongitharm, C. E. Maples, E. C. Leventon, H. H. Strongitharm, R. Bennett, Broad- haw, W. T. Husband, ff. 0. Neilson, T. Cathie W. S. Callender. J. Glover, Johnson, J. C. Crawford. G. E. Sayce and Robert Madge (secretary.) A letter was read from Mr. 0. Holbrook Gaskell, senior, who said advancing years made it incumbent on him to re- frain from attending public meetings. Need he say that it would be very painful to him to appear on a political platform at Widnes in opposition to the son of his old partner, who was himself an intimate friend of his (Mr. Gaskell's) ; but were he Ma own son he should be bound to cast his vote against him so long as he maintained Mr. Gladstone's Irish policy, which he believed would he in effect both dangerous to England and disastrous to Ireland. Among other evils resulting from an Irish Parliament would he an intense aggravation of the con- fre-s between Protestants and Catholics in Ireland. An Irish Parliament would be a Roman Catholic Parliament influenced and controlled by the Irish priesthood. The Protestant Noneonformists of Inland had appealed to their brethren in Great Britian to save them from such a calamity, and he could not believe that they would turn a deaf ear to them. As to the land question the Irish tenant farmer was the most petted and protected by legislation-of any dais in Christendom. (Applause.) And if only he were left in peace and quiet for a few years, to the steady exercise of thrift and industry he would become a prosperous and contented man. This was preciaely what the professional political agitator was striving to prevent. (Applause.) The Chairman said Mr. Moss had been twice returned to Parliament by a triumphant majority, and they were preparing to return him again. (Applause) But he must not conceal from them that they had got the hardest fight befere them that they had ever had. Mr. Deacon —(applause)—was a young man against whom nothing could be said. Be had the respect of everyone in Wid- nes, and if he had come forward a few years before he might have been a formidable opponent indeed. fie was not quite sure that the men of Widnes would now be so inclined to return Mr. Deacon. The very fact of his now being at liberty to contest the division,and of his having more to do with Widnes, would, the speaker thought act as a power against them returning him. (Applause.) Still, he was a most formidable opponent, and it would require their united exertions to keep their member to his present position of pre-eminence. Mr. Richard Lewis moved a resolution of confidence in Mr. Moss.—Mr. Jas. White seconded, and said they could give Mr. Deacon twelve months' start and yet beat him at the winning post. Mr. Moss, who on rising to reply was received with loud cheers, after thanking the audience for their flatter- ing reception, said his opponents in the many meetings they had held had failed to discover an explanation or definition of the policy which they called Home Rule. Be did not think they could define a policy about which they did not know much, and how could they explain a scheme which the grand old leader had not yet framed and the details of which would depend very much upon tie result of the next election? (Applause.) Was it not a fact that all the English Gladstonian subjects tended to show that they were prepared to concede to Ire- land was a legislature which would deal with purely local matters such as a municipality might deal with ? And was it not also a fact that all the Irish speeches tended to show that what the Irishmen ex- pected, and what they intended to get if they could was practically an independent Parliament. as independent as the parliament ofiCanada or Australia? (Applause.) If Mr. Gladstone were returned to power he must disappoint one section or the other of his follow- ers, and he wished to know which side was to be deceived. The Unionist Party maintained that it was ab,lolutely impossible to devise a scheme which would be sufficiently wide to satisfy the national aspirations of the Irish, and not at the same time affect the supremacy of the Imperial Parliament, and the integrity of the United Kingdom. (Applause.) The Unionist party were in favour of giving a measure of local government, and the government had brought in such a measure, but it did ii ,t go far enough to satisfy the Irish Nationalists, and it might possibly go too far for some of their Tory friends. What he maintained was that it was a com- promise which the electors of this country at file last election decided to be a fair and safe compromise, and the details of which they left the pre- sent Government in due time to arrange. (Applause.) Hp hoped this bill would be passed ,and if it were not, he trusted it would be referred to the country, and he felt certain that, with the experience of the last six years, the country would decide again as they did in 1886. (Applause.) It was for the electors to decide whether the present Government should be returned to power; and the good results of Mr. Balfour's rule be continued; or whether they would yield to the cry of Horne Rule and do away with all the good, undermine the feelings of confidence and security which had been created, and throw Ireland back many years in the history of her civilisation. (Applause.) The speaker mentioned the list of reforms carried out by the Govern- ment, and expressed the opinion that had the Home Rule party been in power not one of these mea- sures would have been passed. Alluding to the coal strike, he said he recognised the right of any body of omen to combine Uvrether and take any action to improve their position. (Applause.) He was perfectly aware of the good that Trades Unions had done in the past, and of the power and good they possessed for the future, but he thought that in taking action the members of these unions should not forget their fellow workmen, ,(Applause) and they should try to avoid doing anything which might bring ruin or trouble to men in other trades, whose lot may be no lees hard than their own. (Applause.) He hoped at some future time to deal more fully with this question. He had heard of distress being caused in Widnes by the employment of foreign labour in preference to English labour. If it were true that this distress had been caused by the immigration of foreign paupers, and that they were ousting the British workman from his livelihood, then, he said, why should not pauper immigration be stopped ? Parliament could not perhaps do much in questions relating to labour without interfering with rise liberty of the individual, but Parliament could in- terfere in a question of this kind, and he did not see why foreign countries should be allowed to send paupers here to interfere with British Trade. (Applaus..) In conclusion Mr. Moss expressed the opinion that if they worked hard and worked together they would win again at the next election. Mr. H. Hornby moved and Mr. A. MacKenzie Smith seconded a vote of confidence in the Government, and Mr. T. B. Hoyden, M.P., replied. A vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the pro- ceedings.

div.p: PENKET.EI.

LECTURE BY MR. WHITRHELD.—In connection with the Wesleyan Band of Hope, Mr. W. H. White- head, the renowned vocalist, organist, &c., paid an- other visit to Penketh, after a two years' tourinthe United States, Canada, New Zealand, and Australia. The announcement of the visit attracted a large audience, the room being crowded. Mr. Garnett occupied the chair. The subject of Mr. Whitehead's lecture was" Round the world in a chariot of song," and was illustrative of his recent travels abroad. In au able and graphic manner the various places visited were described, the lecture being inter- spersed by a number of suitable songs. The even- ing was enlivened by a number of humorous anec- dotes, which were much appreciated. At the close a hearty vote of thanks was unanimously accorded Mr. Whitehead, and the meeting dispersed.

div.head: DOUBLE EXECUTION AT OXFORD.
div.p: DOUBLE EXECUTION AT OXFORD.

Frederick Ezgleton and Charles Raynor, who were convicted of the murder of Joseph Ctawley and William Puddyshatt, night watchers, at Pitstone, near Aylesbury on December 12th, were hanged in Oxford Gaol on Thursday morning. Billington was the executioner. He pinioned the men at five minutes to eight, and they thanked the chief warder and chaplain. The pro- cession then formed, the:chaplain reading the service. Raynor went first, the warders followed, and then Eg,gleton. The men wore the same clothes as at the trial. After traversing a corridor for fifteen yards, the long drop was reached. Both men took their places ' under the beam, displaying great firmness. In half-a. minute the bolt was drawn, and the men disappeared. There was no perceptible movement of the bodies after- wards. The Press were admitted.
Nine men, among whom was an engraver, have been arrested at Barcelona for having manufactured false notes of the bank ot France.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

A SOLDIER WANTS TO RE DISCHARGED—AN TJNYROVIDED- I FOR WIFE. A respectable-looking young soldier, named Thomas Southern, was charged, at the Warrington Borough Court, on Monday, with having stolen from the stall of John Morton, in the Market-place, a pair of trousers valued at ss. 6d. ; and also a 41b loaf, the property ef John Gandy, of Pinners-brow. When arrested, the pti- soner said he had stolen the articles because he wanted to be discharged from the army. A sergeant from the barracks stated that prior to his desertion and subse- quent incarceration in prison, Southern had been one of the best characters in the regiment, but since then he had given all the trouble he possibly could. The pri- soner said he had married while in the army, against the regulations. His wife was now at Earlestown, de- pendent upon friends, and he could not keep her as a soldier, and he did not want to see her starve. He was sent to gaol for one month's hard labour.

- - ASSAULTING A LAMPLIGHTER. At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Joseph Prudham, W. Peaks, and Joseph Heaton were charged *with assaulting, at Newton, on the 26th ult., James Kenton, a lamplighter employed by the Newton Im- provement Commissioners. Mr. J. E. Worsley, of War- rington, appeared for the prosecution and Mr. Stuart, of Newton, for the defente. Mr. Worsley said the com- plainant, about half-past 11 on the night of the 26th ult., went to turn out the street lamps, and whilst pro- ceeding on his round was attacked by the three defen- dants. One of them kicked him, and another struck him in the mouth, knocking out a tooth and loosening several others. The complainant struck Heaton in self- defence with his lamp-lighting rod. The matter was reported to the Commissioners, and they ordered that the defendants he prosecuted, and that Mr. Worsley be instructed to appear for the complainant, as they were determined te protect their servants from such outrages. —James Kenton gave corroborative evidence, as also did William Willis, Police-Sergeant Longworth, and John Naylor.—Mr. Stuart contended that there was no case. —The defendants stated that one of them merely spoke to complainant, and he turned round and first assaulted them, and they only struck him in self-defence. The lamp-rod was broken by him over the back of one of them.—Prudham and Heaton were fined 10s. and costa each, and Peake was dismissed ; and cross-summonses taken out against Kenton for assault were also dismissed. THEFT OF LEAD. At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Tuesday, Peter Fernley was charged with stealing on the 10th inst., 59 lbs. of lead, the property of the National Tele- phone Co., Orford Street. P.C. 'Brewin deposed that he was informed that the prisoner had been seen going into the prosecutors' yard, and he went there and after an hour's search, found the prisoner secreted there with the lead lying near him. He said it was a drunken spree. —He was fined 103. including costs. THEFT OF A CAP. At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Wednes- day, Edward Williams, labourer, was charged with steal- ing, on the previous night, a cap, the property of Mr. Egerton, hatter, 104 Bridge-st. Detective-Sergeant Monaghan said he saw the man hanging about various shops in a suspicious way, and go to Egerton's shop door and put under his coat a cap hanging there. He fol- lowed him and asked him what he had upon him. He ran along past the Lion Hotel palisadings. He was ar- rested, and the cap was found behind the railings. He was sent to prison for 14- days. A TwerT BY BOYS. At the Warrington County Sessions on Wednesday, George Kaye and Charles Hughes, two small boys, were charged withstealing at Sankey Bridges, on. the 3rd inst. a leather belt, the property of Thomas Garner,' of Bold, near Widnes. The prosecutor, a boy, said he was with a horse and cart, and missed the belt from the horse's bridle. He found that that had been stolen by the pri- soners. He spoke to Kay about it, and he said Hughes took it ;he would take anything he could lay hands on. —A police constable said Kay told him that he bought the belt from Hughes, and Hughes that he stole it.—The lad pleaded guilty.—Kay was sentenced to four strokes of the birch rod, and Hughes, who was the younger boy, to six strokes. STEALING A SAW AND AN UMBRELLA. At the Warrington Borough Magistrates' Court, on Thursday, Elijah Hillman, glass maker, of 202, Longford street, was charged with stealing on the Bth ult., from a building in course of erection in Mount-street, a saw the property of James George joiner, 17, Ellersley-street, Manchester-road, also with stealing on the 3rd of May, 1891, from Axpley-street Station, an umbrella, the pro- • perty of C. Ashurst, stationmaster, at Bank Quay. Mr. Browne appeared for the defendant. The articles were discovered by D.S. Mocaghari and Inspector Spinks on the 16th ult., at his house. The prisoner said he had bought the saw from a man in Dudley, and the umbrella from a stall in the market.—Mr. Browne pleaded guilty on behalf of the prisoner. He said he had just been in prison more than a month for another offence. He had a wife and family, and had been out of work a couple of months, and he (Mr. Browne) asked the Bench on behalf of his client's wife and family to treat the case with great leniency.—He was fined 10s. including costs, in each case. CHARGE OF CRUELTY TO CHILDREN. At the Warrington Borough police Court, yesterday, the case of Joseph Benson, 8, Ship Yard, charged with wilfully neglecting his children which was before the court some time since,and adjourned, was announced by the deputy-magistatcs' clerk to be withdrawn. SELLING ADULTERATED MILE. Thomas Allen, milk dealer, 5, Pitt-st., was charged at the Warrington Borough Police Court, by Inspector Nor- man, with selling on ,the 4th inst., milk adulterated with 10 per cent, of water.—Mr. Norman proved purchasing the milk and having it analysed by the county analyst.— The defendant was fined 20s. and Costs. THEFT BY A GIRL. At the Warrington Borough Magistrates' Court, yester- day morning, Ellen Aplin, aged 12, daughter of John Aplin, Welfield-st, was charged with stealing, on the Wednesday pravious, one lady's chemise, one child's chemise, one toilet cover, and one tablecloth, the pro- perty of David Walton, 11, Lovely-lane. It appeared that the girl had been in the habit of going to the com- plainant's house to sell cakes, and had taken the oppor- tunity to steal the articles. She pawned the articles at Mr. Briggs's, for Is., and tore up the ticket. Some one picked up the pieces, and took them to him, and he was suspicious, and informed the police, and she was arrested.—The prosecutor begged that she might be bound over only.—She pleaded guilty, and was fined 10s., including costs, in default seven days. CRUELTY TO A MAIL COACH HORSE. Yesterday, at the Warrington Borough Police Court, George Clegg, driver, in the employ of Messrs. Wood, Brothers, contractors for the driving of the mail coach between Liverpool and Manchester was charged with ill-treating, by working it while in an unfit state, one of the horses drawing the mail coach ; and Taylor, of Prescct, horsekeeper for Messrs. Wood, was charged with causing the horse to be so worked.—Mr. Forshaw appeared for both defendants. Inspector Dowty, R.S.P.C.A., deposed to finding wounds on three horses drawing the coach though he only proceeded as to one f the horses. The wounds were so had that it was otterly unfit for work.—James Wood, Mr. Horrocks, uaterinary surgeon, of Manchester, and James Taylor, vaveevidence that the animal was quite fit.—The Bench gned the defendants 208. and costs each. a

It was stated that he had brcken a lamp which was valued at 63. 6d. The ease was dismissed,as it was stated that the lad's parents had promised to pay the amount of the damage. TENANTS' RESPONSIBILITIES.—A number of persons living in Rose-yard and Cockhedge-lane, named Carr Ellison, Rooney, Hynes, Bates, and Broderick, were summoned at the instance of the Sanitary Committee for having neglected to keep their pail closets in a clean and fit state. Inspector Norman gave evidence for the prosecution. They were each fined 2s. 6cl. THREATENING A MOTHER.—ThOMIS Walsh, a strong looking young man, was charged with unlawfully threatening his mother. Mrs. Walsh deposed that her son wanted some money from her and as she would not give him it he used the threat complained of towards her. Ile was bound over in two sureties of £lO each to keep the peace. BREACHES OF THE l'sacn.—Catherine Hynes was charg- ed with having been drunk and disorderly in Hill-street, on the Bth March, and also with committing a breach of the peace by assaulting Harriet Daintith. She was fined 59.—Mary Cody and!Agnes Jackson, mother-in-law and daughter-in-law, were charged with having committed a breach of the peace by fighting with each other, and were each ordered to pay costs. TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. R. Garnett (chairman), E. J. Guest, and W. Owen. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—George Donoghue, in Horsemarket-St., on Monday morning, ss. SCHOOL CASES.—At the instance of Mr. Riley, school attendance officer, the following were dealt with for not sending their children regularly to school i—William France, brewer, Watkin-st., 2s. 61 ; Michael Lawless, labourer, Hardy-st., is. ; Sarah Maxfield, Bewsey- road, is. ; Thomas Moody, forgeman, Pierpoint-st., 53. ; Thomas Newhall, gas stoker, Mersey-st., 23. 6d. In the case of Patrick Carey,forgeman, Dolman's-lane, an order was made for his son to be sent to Father Nugent's school.—William Armitage, forgeman, Orforcalane, 2s. 6d. ; Edward Bretherton, brewer, Wa.tkin-st., 2s. 6d. WEDNESDAY.—Before Councillor Jas. Faircloua,h, Alder- man Wright, and Mr. E. M. Crcsfield.

DRUNK.—Patrick Grady, a soldier at Orford Barracks, was charged with being drunk on Tuesday night, in Orford-Si., and dismissed on promising tv keep sober in future. THURSDAY.—Before Captain Ridgway (chairman), and Councillor Jas. Fairclough. DRUNKENNESS AND OBSTRUCTION.—Edward Burke,rub- bing stone hawker, 11th appearance, was charged with being drunk and disorderly the previous night in Win- wick-st., also with not appearii.g to a summons charg- ing him with causing an obstruction in Scotland-road, on May 16th, by allowing his horse and cart to stand unnecessarily long. D. S. Monoghan, P.S. Chantler,and others gave evidence in the first case, from which it ap- peared that he was driving a pony and 'cart furiously and nearly ran over several people. He was fined 10s. and costs, £1 3s. in all. FRlDAY.—Before Councillor Voisey, C.C., (chairman), and Alderman Wriligt. THE MAGISTRATES LITE AGAIN.—The commencement of the business was delayed about half-an-hour in con- sequence of there being no magistrate present. NON-MAINTRNANCE ON THE OLlO.—Alfred Birchall, 31, Silver-square, charged with non-payment of arrears of contributions for maintenance of his son on board the Clio, was committed for 14 days.—Joseph Smith, 18. DRUNIK.—George Farmer, drunk on the 27th ult., was fined 2s. 6d. and costs. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Joseph Bedall, at Sankey Bridges, on Saturday night, was fined 2s. 6d.—Joseph Brimelow, at Martinscroft, on the 27th ult., ss. and costs. Bionwev OFFENCES.—DanieI Oliver, for bicycling on the footpath at Cuerdley, on the 20th ult.,who had corn- mitted the offence to avoid stones on the road, was ordered to pay costs.—Reuhen Wilson, of Warrington, was charged with being asleep in charge of a horse and cart at Rixton, on the night of the 7th inst. He had, a constable said, smashed into an egg cart. Ho was fined 2s. 6d. and costs.

div.head: "MARGIT, WE RUN PART !"
div.p: "MARGIT, WE RUN PART !"

Wen sarcumstances cum to change The faytures of a caQe, It's allus best to be a molt, An' meet um face to face. Aw've hed a shock— aw'mdeawnrigh till— Cowd shivers through me dart, Thi feyther winnot " post the blunt," So, Margit, we mull part! Th' owd stingy beggar ! an' he sez His bank is welly broke; He cannot tell me fieaw he feels, For fear ez he should choke. He sez he winnot let thi leave— 'Twud welly breyk his heart ; An' so, theau sees, it cums to this— My Margit, we mun part! Aw moan't play footebaw! fer he swears It's one o' th' ferbidden sins To leg a brother deawn. an' then Pev'l at his ribs an' shins! No wench o' his mun see her mon Browt mangl't in a cart; But ez aw meean to pleaze mysel, Why, Margit, we mun part! He wants me t' turn teetotal too, An' drink nowt else but pop; An then he'd mebbe change his mind, An' start Us in a shop! But aw'mnoan gooin't be T. T.,— Aw've sworn it too, by th' art; He isn't beaun to brew my drink, So, Margit, we mull part! Oh, have aw follow'd thi for this, An. hey aw spent my brass, To make thi allus preawd o' me, An' then turn eawt a ass ! Nowe, nowe ! awll noan heed him, shuz heaw It makes my gizzert smart ; It's aw U—P!—eawr gam' is up My Margit, we mun part! Fareweel, owd craytur ! never moor Shall aw behowd thy smile; No moor thi coaxin' ways on me My agony shall pile. Fareweel ! for Wiggin's amooky clime, To-morrow morn aw'll start; An' aw becoze, my Margit dear, The feyt her wudn't part!
Nyowton, God bless 0,19, 3, '92.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 19, 1892.

Heesom luckily charged. John Bate was hurt at this point of the game, but the visitors generously allowed Thorailey to make up the required number, Berry going half back. Abrams responded to a kick, and play settled at Warrington quarter flag, Donohue charging a kick of Davies. Play was on the half way line, when some brilliant passing by James Bate and Berry, Evans, and Heesom saw the centre transferring to Webster, who failed to take a bad pass. Give and take play ensued, but a bril- liant dribble by Massey and Hampson changed the scene to Warrington quarters. Davies was well tackled by Heesom, and then another tricky run by the Run- cornian saw Boscow tackling in true style. Runcorn still attacked, but Evans eased matters a trifle by a lofty kick and tackle of Abrams. Berry and Bate changed the venue to half-way. Some neat play was shown by Riley, but Turner spoiled progress by making his mark. Anotbee brilliant piece of work by Davies saw Boscow at his best, and a moment later another fine kick of the home custodian took play to neutral ground. From a scrimmage at centre, Bate ran clean down to Houghton, and passing to Webster, the latter only travelled five yards when he was pulled up. Berry was applauded for a fine kick, but Bandies was a shade for- ward when a good chance presented itself. Runcorn, too eager, lost a lot of ground from Turner's free kick, which landed the oval at half way. Some passing by the home halves was foiled by Abrams, whilst the last-named was conspicuous in breaking up a rush of the home forwards. A smart run by Robinson was seconded by Davies, but Bcscow was safe. Eventually a penalty kick wag awarded the visitors, and Houghton forced a minor. The drop out saw play at half way, and some loose scrambling play followed. Turner led the home- eters beyond the half way, and repeatedly Warrington forwards sv heeled tha scrimmage in fine style, only to see Abrams on the alert and break up the combination. Gradually Runcorn forced their way to the Warrington end. A dribble, headed by Berry and Thorniley, again placed the sides on even terms, but Riley failed to mani- pulate a chance, and Webster saved. Some fine drib- bling of the Cheshire men almost ended in a score ; whilst passing bout by the Runcorn backs saw Ileesom tackling Davies accurately. The interval was now called with no substantial score. Turner re-started ,and a ponderous kick by Houghton landed the oval at half way. Dolan ran round the scrisnmage,but Bate had him before he travel- led far. Houghton kicked brilliantly at this juncture, but neither side could claim a distinct advantage. A sharp dribble by Hampson and Riley saw play almost on the home line", but Webster came to the rescue with a flying kick, Evans accounting for Davies. Play, however, was at the Warrington quarter flag, and although a temporary cessation of the attack was brought about by Berry, Houghton again punted finely, and the threatened attempt of Warrington to invade was frustrated. Bate got away again, though the effort did not realise many yards. but a fine piece of play by Webster proved too much for Houghton. Bandies next got away from a line out, and play was taken to the visitors' lines. A rush by Williams and Shaw gained a few yards, and Houghton and Boscow exchanged kicks, play finally resting at the Runcorn quarter flag, the Warring- tonians fumbling when a chance was presented them. Webster recovered the lost ground, and Houghton saved. Jolley met the drop out, and Gayter was smart in staying the progrcss of Jolley and Berry, whilst a dribble by Bate SAW Houghton saving daringly. From a scrimmage near the line Thorniley reached over and scored near the corner. Turner failed at goal. Again Warrington pressed, and Heesorn obliged with the finest run of the day. The homesters would not be denied, and putting on pressure, the Runcorn defece was again broken through, and Evans scored near the corner on the popular side, Turner making a grand bid for goal. Runcorn's defence, with the exception of Houghton, became weaker as time approached, but Warrington failed to augment thex score, which stood at the close as two tries and three minors to Runcorn one minor. It was a clinking game, every art which goes to make I the code a success being requisitioned. Runcorn, des- I pite the fact that their combination suffered by the ab- sence of several who have well nigh brought it to per- fection, played splendidly. They had a deal the best of it in the first half, but tired terribly near the close, and it was then that Warrington's stamina asserted itself, and the day was won. Houghton was a splendid back, as also was Boscow. Both centres were a creditable pair, Abrams being prominent in saving, whilst Heesom tackled safely. Davies and Evans were the pick of the three-quarters, and of the forwards Massey, Riley, Hampson, Turner, Jolley, and Buckley were the best.
THE HEALTH OF MRS. OSBORNE.

--- Since her trial, Mrs. Osborne has 'shown a decided improvement. She still remains in the infirmary, and appears far more cheerful than before. In accordance with the prison regulations, however, her friends will not be allowed to visit her for some weeks.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

",," Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning. RUGBY. WinNas V. TOTTINGTON.—PIayed at the latter place on Saturday, and the home team won by one goal to nil. The visitors were poorly represented. RUNCORN v. BIRKENHEAD PARK.—Frost and snow made it impossible for Runcorn to meet Birkenhead Park, in the Cheshire championship football match, on Saturday. The visitors arrived in town, expecting there might be a bare possibility of engaging in the encounter, but on examination they came to the decision that the ground was in an unfit condition. WARRINGTON Y. BRIGHOUSE RANGERS. The above-mentioned clubs met for the first time at Brighouse on Saturday. At one period of the week it was doubtful whether the match would take place, but the Rangers' executive were energetic on the morning of the match, and relieving the ground of its white mantle, their efforts were rewarded by seeing a large gate, which numbered close on 4,000. The ground is one of the most peculiar in the north, sloping to the extent of nearly two feet from goal to goal, and that Brighouse are no mean adepts on their native heath may be judged from the large nurtber of matches they have won there. For Saturday's match Nichol, the inter- national, was an absentee; but Warrington had got a good team together, Davies supplanting Buckley from the original team selected. It was 3.20 when Ward kicked off up the slope, play being confined to the forwards for the first five minutes, and at neutral ground. A kick from Heesom, and Jolley intercepting a pass to Wilson, the Tykes' quarter flag was reached, Waddington coming with a host of Warrington forwards round him. Evans made his mark in response to Abbey, but the home custodian and East- wood kicking strongly, and Boscow failing to reply, Warrington had an exceptionally warm time of it. The home forwards revelled in what was now a quagmire, the field almost representing a sea of mud. Croft wat to the fore in a dribble, but Turner, Teare, and Dono- hue, in one rush, and Berry and Davies in another, placed the sides on level footing once more at half way. Webs- ter got in a kick at close quarters, whilst Berry and Jolley drove with another dribble, which Brooke nipped in the bud, and freed the game at the top of the slope. A penalty kick to Warrington for wilful infringement by Wilson did net realize much, for the kick was responded to by Wood, whose smart footwork changed the venue. Give-and-take play had been the order, but for a time Brighouse now acted on the aggressive. Evans and Heesom were both sound in their defence, although it is only fair to state the Bates were hampered by a set of half backs who ridiculed the "on-side" law. Jagger, Sugden, and Hughes were foremost in another combined dribble of the homesters ; but Warrington, despite the keenness with which the Tykes maintained their advantage, disputed every inch of ground manfully. James and John Bate passed neatly for the first time, but Heesom's kick was more than neutra- lized by Brooke. Armitage next headed the Bangers to the line, whilst Donohue, 'Nate, and Ashton were next engaged in a like capacity for Warrington, and the move- ment reaching the Rangers' twenty-five flag, Jolley was held in close proximity to the line. Heeso in supplemented smart passing by the Bates, but Webster was foiled, and the game again went in the Rangers' favour. "Smack" Bate tackled his opponent (Oakes) in fine style, and ran half the length of the field before passing to Webster, but the transfer was a shade forward. Again Bate got cleverly away from a pass by John Bate, and the move- ment realized a pretty exhibition by Turner, Bandies, and Donohue. A minor was next credited to Brighouse, whilst a second was forthcoming directly after. From this point Warrington took up the attack, Berry running fling and tackling Brooke, and finally Heesom in an effort was held under the posts. A minor accrued, but War- rington returned to the attack once more, and, after Boscow had screwed to touch, Davies and Ashton were prominent in some loose play. Near the call of time Jolley made a bid for honours, but, being deprived near ' the line, passed to Evan: who completeda well-deserved try. Turner failed at a difficult place. Half-time was next called, with the score :—Wa'rrington, 0-1-1 ; Brighouse Rangers 0-0-3. Turner re-started, and Armitage ran and passed to Earnshaw, who was grassed when becoming dangerous. Ilopton and Wood dribbled well, and Boscow and Evans were forced to save in succession. Heesom was floored in trying to relieve, whilst Croft was awarded a mark when fully a dozen hands were round him. The easy place was not augmented by Abbey. Turner steer- ing the oval a foot outside the posts. Warrington still had the worst of it, Taylor and Armitage both experiencing hard lines. A flying kick by Webster eased the attack a little, but a long kick by Eastwood registered the fifth minor of the match. Some exchanges between Handles, Boscow, Brooke, and Abbey ended in favour of the hornesters, whilst from a pass by Wilson, Brooke was held under the posts. A mistake by Webster almost cost his side a try, but the forwards, working well to a man, rushed down the popular side, and trans- ferred play to neutral ground. Eventually a kick trav- elled to Waddington, who screwed across to Eastwood, who, in the opinion of many, was waiting off-side, and taking the oval in clean style, he galloped over the line in a position whio.li allowed Abbey to augment. The Warringtonians stoutly protested against the legitimacy of the try, but it was of no avail, and there-start took place from centre. Warrington now rallied, avid at once forced matters. Heesom took a pass from John Bate in fine style, whilst some rushing business by Jolley and Davies landed the oval on the line. A spell of pretty passing was witnessed between the Bate:, Evans, and Heesom, Abbey staving off the well-meant effort. Davies saved in daring manner, whilst a moment later Jolley threw to Webster, who was promptly floored. The last- named next had a fine chance with a clear field, but failed to gather the oval. When near the call of time, Heesom made a bold bid, but was held when within an arm's reach of the line, and Warrington had eventually to retire defeated by a goal and six miners to a try and a minor. Teams :—Warrington : J. Boscow, back; H. Webster- F. Heesom, and I. W. Evans, three-quarter backs ; James Bate and John Rate, half backs; H. Ashton Fair. Turner, J. Jolley, W. Bandies, H. Teare, T. Davies, J. T. Thorni- ley, T. Donohue, and J. Berry, forwards. Brighouse Rangers Abbey, back ; Eastwood, Brooke, and Waddington, three-quarter backs ; Oates and Wilson, half backs; Wood, Hughes, Jagger, Sugden, Hopton, Croft, Earnshaw, Taylor, and Arinttage, forwards. WARRINGTON "A" V. STOCKPORT " A."—There was considerable interest taken in this encounter, but the uncertainty as to whether the match could be played affected the gate. Warrington commenced the contest, on ground partly covered with snow, and Antrobus passing out splendidly, a minor resulted from a drop at goal. Then Stockport experienced an anxious few minutes through the fast work of Hampson, Barnes, Higham, and Warburton, but relief came when Smith , kicked dead. Following this, matters assumed a more even aspect, until over real exhibited on the part of the home team gave the visitors a foothold inside the ' quarter flag. Some very smart work on the part of the Antrobus and Hall staved off any attempts at scoring, but all the value of Ashurst's fine kick was nullified by offside play. A free kick to Warrington was a welcome relief, Hall and Molyneux supplementing this by a dribble to the visitors' quarters. Here Stockport showed their dexterity by some capital passing, but Ashurst re- gained all the lost ground by a splendid kick. Directly afterwards Antrobus stole away beautifully, and passing to Potts, the latter ran over splendidly. Goodall then distinguished himself, and the game gradually worked towards the home stronghold, and when the attackers were looking dangerous, Lally started a movement which was grandly utilized, and Antrobus, picking up, threw wide to Potts, who made a grand dashing run over the line, but losing possession, a miner was allowed. Stock- port again attacked, exhibiting much smartness in the art of passing, but Ashurst, by some finely judged kick- ing, caused hostilities to wage at midfield. Lally here showed up with a capital run. Buckley, Molyneux, Barby, and Glever rushing the leather into the Stock- port half. The visitors then got together, and dribbling down the field had a splendid opportunity of scoring, but failing at a critical moment, the danger was quickly cleared by Barnes, Daniels, Westall, and Hampson, and at half time the score was Warrington 0-1-3 to nil. The brief rest had evidently an inspiriting influence on the combatants, for the fray opened fast and furious, Hampson, Bailey, Kitchen, and Itathbone showing up prominently for their respective sides. More good passing by the Stockport backs was fraught with dan- ger to their opponents, hut the defence was too good, and Westall, Buckley, Glover, and Higham cleared to more desirable territory. A splendid bit of play was then witnessed 'on the part of Antrobus, Lally, and Daniels, and when a score seamed certain, a drop at goal lost the opportunity. Following the drop out, Hampson made a fine dribble to the line, Ashton replying by a counter effort, causing the antagonists to test tha war- fare in neutral territory. Molyneux and Lally returned the oval to the quarter flag, where Hampson effected another dribble to the visitor's citadel, securing a try, Warburton making a rattling attempt to convert. The game, which had been vigorously contested, continued , to be fought with great spirit and robustness, and a splendid bout of passing on the part of Antrobus, Lally Daniels, and Potts harrassed the visitors' defence, a grand strong run by the latter forcing a minor. War- burton and Lawless entirely neutralised the drop out, but nothing mo. 0 was obtained, and a capitally contest- ed encounter ended Warrington 0-2-5 to nil. WARRINGTON (H. ASHTON'S TEAM) v. RUNCORN (W. FAULKNER'S TEAM). The response to the appeal on behalf of the Jolley Memorial Fund was indeed a praiseworthy one, and those who had charge of the affair must have felt that their efforts had not been in vain. The match was played on the Wilderspool ground, on Monday evening.
