div.head: LION TAMER KILLED.
div.p: A LION TAMER KILLED.

A. Wolverhampton correspondent describes a terrible scene in Wombwell and Bailey's Menagerie. An exhibi- tion was being given at fiednesford, and a negro lion tamer named Delhi Montarno slipped while in the act of enbring a cage containing three bears and a hyena, which at once set upon him and worried him for a quarter of an hour, death ensuing within twenty minutes of his removal. At the inquest on Tuesday, Mr. Bostock, the proprieter, stated that he at once entered the cage, but failed for some time to get the animals away.
THE CONFESSION OF MURDER AT WARRINGToN. THE PRISONER DISMISSED.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Saturday, be- fore Aldermen Burgess (chairman) and Chandley and Messrs. IL Garnett and J. Geddes, Rowland Geo. Lush was brought up on remand, charged on his own confession.with having murdered William Par- sons, draper, of Andover, at that place in November, 1858.—The deputy-magistrates' clerk (Mr. G. F. F. White) read a letter from the chief constable of Plamp- shire, statinv, that he had found nothing to corroborate the prisoner's statement. On the contrary, from the re- ports of the case at the time and from additional infor- mation, everything tended to show that Lush could not have been connected with the murder. le did not wish prisoner to be handed over to the Hampshire police, as there was not sufficient evidence even to justify a re- mand. Superintendent Lawler,of the Hampshire police, was present, and in reply to the Chairman, said he had no other information to give.—The Chairman asked the prisoner if he had anything to say, and he replied, "No more than my statements previously."—The prisoner was then dismissed, and left the dock with an air of un- willingness and of disappointment at, or at least no satisfaction with, the result.

div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.

FOOTBALL—RUGBY. Warrington paid a visit to the champion county on Saturday, and met the stout Rangers of Brighouse. Brgihouse being a Yorkshire team, it goes without say- ing that they play vigorously, and put some heavy weight into their scrimmages. In the result,Yorkshire upheld its reputation,though 14y a narrow margin. War- ringtGn were the first to score a try, and it must be said that the similar point which the Yorkshiremen im- proved into a goal 4as strongly disputed on the ground that the player who won it had been off side. However, referees are supreme, and the referee decided that it was all right," and as "all right " it will have to stand upon the record.

Warrington was not by any means the only set of Lancastrians who had to knuckle down to the redoubt- able champions of the broad-acred county. Wigan were defeated at home by Halifax, this being mainly brought about by a droppqd goal. Only 14 men turned out for Wigan, but Slevin stepped into the breach and completed the number. The half-back play ot W. Halliwell was frequently cheered. Huddersfield had easy victims in New Brighton, and St. Helens fell before the rushes of Elland.
ASSOCIATION. It is understood that football professionalism in Scot- land on the same terms as those which obtain in England is likely to be legalized at an early date.

History has repeated itself With regard to the Associa tion Challenge Cup. In 1887 the final tie was fought out by Aston Villa and West Bromwich Albion,and the same two Birmingham clubs will again meet in the last round at the Oval to-day (Saturday). The Albion have had a hard fight in qualifying for the final. They had to meet Nottg Forest no fewer than three times in the "semi," but made no mistake on the third occasion. The Forest were very unlucky in having to face a regular snow- storm for the first quarter of an hour, and never seemed to get over it. Their antagonists opened the scoring early, and ran out conquerors by no fewer than six goals to two. This was a great blow to the Forest, who at the finish lodged a protest on the ground of the in. clemency of the weather, but this has been dismissed, and now the Albion are free to again try their strength against their neighbours from Perry Barr. As the Villa have already beaten the West Bromwich team three times this season and are now stronger than ever, they ought to repeat their victory of five years ago.

--- The question of the League championship of 1891-2 is supposed to have been settled on Saturday last, when the 'North End were easily vanquished at Sunderland. The latter won by four goals to one—the biggest defeat , of the Pre.stonians during the season,—and as they have a much better record than any of their rivals, they can hardly fail to wind up at the top of the list. The match was contested in a snowstorm, and this no doubt kept down the attendance. Still there were about 12,00 spectators present. Despite the assistance of the well-known ama- teur Tinsley Lindley, the forward play of the North End was of a poor quality. The home team were seen at their best, their defence being very safe.

What can be said of the farce enacted at Perry Bar ? Everybody knows that Accrington are much inferior to Aston Villa, but nobody contemplated such a slaughter as 12 to 2. This is the League record of the season, and bodes ill for the prospects of the Albion this week end. West Bromwich had their full cup team at Blackburn, but had the worst of the play by three goals to two. rhe Rovers have thus beaten both the cup finalists with- in eight days. The return League fixture between Dar- win and Burnley had to be postponed owing to the failure of the referee to keep his appointment. A practice game was substituted in which Dar wen added one more to their unbroken list of victories against Burnley at Barley Bank. Ewerton pulled off their return at Stoke, scoring a goal to none for the second time within a week.

So vast was the interest in the final tie for the Scot- tish Cup that 40,000 spectators are said to have been present at Ibrox Park, this being the biggest gate in the history of the game. It was practically a trial of strength between the League champions and Anti- Leaguers. The Celtic are the best club in the League and Queen's Park and the strongest outside that body. As the Queen's had previously beaten Dumbarton and Itenton, both of whom they met twice, their tie with the Celtic awoke unbounded enthusiasm. The Celtic scored a goal to none, but as there were interruptions owing to encroachments by the tremendous crowd the clubs have been ordered by the Scottish Association to re-play the tie on April 9.

Letter to the Obttor.
THE HALF-HOLIDAY MOVEMENT IN WARRINGTON.

Sir,—We, the undersigned members of the association wish to say there is nothing of the nature of a "politi- cal move "in the interests of the Radical party in our movement. We wish respectfully to contradict any assertion to the contrary as being entirely unfounded. The association has nothing whatever to do with any political party. Every public gentleman was invited to attend irrespective of any party or creed.— S. N. GREEN. J. R. STANLEY, A. CLOWES, H. POWELL, Sub-Committee.

Sir,—Now that the movement has been fairly launched and brought so conspicuously before the public by the mass meeting, it will, no doubt interest your readers, and those tradesmen particularly who were not present, just to review the position as at present. For some weeks past some dozen assistants have been meeting in committee, and have been discussing this question in all its bearings, and, sir, the one cardinal
Point always before them has been not to take any step

that would be detrimental to the employers' interest. The question raises many points of contention, just as a man conceives what he considers what ought to be and what ought not to be. If it be that the half-holiday is

suitable to the ninety and nine of the tradesmen, then, surely, for the sake of the assistants why net the odd one fall in with the movement ? it were the law of the country to close a half day per week, then we should hear nothing whatever of these ob- jections that are raised against the movement. I heartily wish, sir, that we had had many more trades- men present:.. We sent out 480 circulars and distributed

2,506-handbills, 1,000 leaflets, and posted the town, and the response was far beyond our expectation. rhe letters of sympathy are very numerous, and a majority of tradesmen are already waiting to grant this boon. But, sir, we want every shop closed • we want every assistant in Warrington to enjoy his or her half holiday, and we intend to urge upon every tradesman the desir- ability of considering this question natil out of the feel- ings of his heart he grants to his assistants the privilege and pleasures of a half holiday. It is a singular fact that every member of the Committee is virtually in posses- ion of a half holiday with one or two exceptions, but the desire which prevails is for every assistant to enjoy a little privilege. Now, Sir, I sum up thus that all ironmongers, clothiers hairdressers, boot establishments, hatters and pawn- brokers, are going to adopt the half-holiday with an ex- ception here and there, and so I may say that almost the same prevails amongst drapers, provision dealers, and grocers. What we want is one grand effort to commence on the 24th day of March. I cannot do better than bring my letter, (which has already taken up so much of your valuable space) to a close, by quoting the motto of the Association " Surely the Assistant's welfare is the Master's interest."-1 am, dear sir, yours truly, S. N. GREEN, Treasurer of Assistants' Association.

Sir,—Having read the account of last week's meeting, I should like to offer a few remarks on the subject. Among a number of letters sent expressing sympathy with the movernont,l noticed one from Messrs. Eustance, Jewellers, Sankey-st. Perhaps the public will better appreciate their sympathy wheal state that on the last Bank holiday (December 26th, 1891), when all the other jewellers were closed, Messrs. Eustance thought that a fitting opportunity to open their shop. I was surprised to read the remarks of Mr. Thomas Morris. I fear he must have been mixing with some wicked Radical 3 to judge by the language he used. According to Mr. Kent, the poor shop assistants have no holidays at all, and yet I have always understood they were allowed not less than a week or ten days every summer, in addition to which there are four Bank holidays, besides Christmas day, Good Friday, and Walking day, not amiss for one year in my opinion. Of course Councillor Henry Roberts was to the fore as usual, and, if he did not say anything very convincing, he made up for argument in condemming those who differed from him. I wonder if it is intended to extend the half-noliday to the assis- tants of the British Workman Company, and, if not, must they be boycotted accordingly ?—I are yours Szc, JOHN JONES. 13ewsey-street, March lath 1892.

div.head: OUR COMMISSIONERS AGAIN!
div.p: OUR COMMISSIONERS AGAIN!

^Sir,—Whenever I want to indulge in a little comic literature, I don't, as you might suppose, fly to "Punch, or "Judy," or "Fun". No, I have a better mark than any of these. Igo to your columns, and read the doings of our Commissioners, and there find ample food, both for fun and for reflection. The fun comes in, or rather came in, last week, when I saw the delegates who were appointed to select horses, •tc., for removing the night- soil. I wonder, sir, if there is more than one of their number knows as much about a horse as a China,rnan knows of Chovvbent—always excepting the Rocking Horse on which they were wont in childhood's days to " ride to Banbury Cross !" The Government principle seems to be their guide; for it is well known that it must be a civilian who shall regulate military matters; and a man who has "never smelt salt water" is always considered the fittest to manage our Men of War. When the "Destructor" question cropped up, it was decided to send three mechanical "experts "to assist the furveyor in corning to a correct decision ; and the men selected were "the very largest ratepayer," a pub- lican, and a draper! Talk about putting round pegs in square brAQS!! But absurdity didn't end there. They went on improving; and on the question of horses, ijudges among themselves were appointed, and all—save one—having but small experience of the "noble quad- rimed." the chances are that we shall have tramping our streets, "brutes that would be dear at five dollars" —three cornered beasts in shape not unlike a projected Public Hall we all wot of! "both angular and flat !" —animals, on which our very careful Police Sergeant will always have an anxious eye; and on which, to ride barebadked for a mile or two would be a punishment compared to which the pillory were a mere nothing. • Think of it, brother and sister ratepayers! Try and realize the picture of each of these " experts" mounted on their purchases, and riding in procession through the village'l Why, you wouldn't miss it—l know I wouldn't—for any money. And yet, that we shall be blessed with the sort of brute .I have described above, unless common-sense comes to their rescue, and they have the modesty to leave the matter to the only one vita° knows something of horses,—,is about as plain as that Church Bells and Foundry Buzzers carrbe,and often are, an untold nuisance! Thank a merciful Providence, there will soon be a chance of relegating some of these "experts" to their proper sphere—a sphere they would never have left, if they had put a true measure on their own perspicacity ! That the chance may not be lost is the humble and fervent prayer nf yours truly, RIGDUM FUNNYDUSr. Earlectown., 16, 3, M 92.

LANDLORD'S RENTS AND -MINERS' WAGES. Sir,—There is a decided disposition in certain quarters to lay the blame apon the wrong shoulders in the great' coal crisis through which we are now passing. The fact that the miners have of late years bee* the recipients of considerable advances upon their former wages is being used as an argument in favour of their nubmission to a certain reduction now. But the real point to consider is not whether their wages are higker than they used to be, bat whether theyare higher than they ought to be. If we take into account the heavy labour which he nridergoe;, ' and the serious risk to width lie is exposed, we must all admit that the miner is certainly not overpaid, and no just man, however inconvenienced hy the great strike, ought to ,blame the men for trying to avert the eontem- plated reduction. Let us admit that aome of the eni- ployers are wider the necessity of effect/04g a eaving in their workitig,expenses. We lICA nit th-erefore admit that they are loomed to pay less wages to Weir workmen. Ate .41/9 sjAie,r ,i,teAs of expense in the ;mining fadustry,

as in every other, are rent and wages. How is it that capitalists invariably seek first to economise in the latter rather than in the former? Why should the miner be asked to take less while the landlord takes the same? Here is the root of the whole difficulty.

It may not be generally known that every ton of coal extracted from the bowels of the earth bears, in the shape of royalty, dead-rent, wayleave, an average tribute of no less than ninepence to the landowner. In Germany and France the royalty is less than twopence a ton, and that is paid to the State, and thus lessens taxa- tion. This is the ideal system—State ownership of the minerals and a fair and revisable royalty payable to the public revenue- But until we get this we ought to have employers and employed working together for the re- duction of the heavy landlord dues which now so seri- ously cripple this great foundation industry. "An Ironmaster " gives his own case in to-day's papers. He will have to blow out his furnaces and pay off his men for lack of fuel if the strike continues. But he doesn't blame the miners. He reminds ifs that his output of 50.000 tons of pig-iron pays no less than £15,000 a year in royalties to private individuals. Yet the wages of all the men he employs only amount to £7,500 yearly. The landlords of England derive an annual income of about £10,000,000 from the minerals which were created countless years ago, and which are practically a neces- sity of our individual and national existence. This amount is considerably in excess of reasonableness, and the present coal crisis has been occasioned by the failure on the part of both masters and men to realise it with sufficient clearness. I sincerely hope that public atten- tion will be widely directed to this phase of the question and that this great industrial war may show miners and mineowners,and all other classes of the community, that the real enemy which leads now and always to such a grievous paralysis of industry is in reality the monopoly of Nature's products by private individuals.—Yours faithfully, lOSEPH FIYDER.

Land Nationalisation Society, 14, Southhampton-street, Strand, London. [P.S.—I shall be pleased to send literature upon the question of Mining Royalties to any of your readers who wish to know the lull facts of the case. -- WARRINGTON AND THE FORTHCOMING

div.head: ELECTION.
div.p: ELECTION.

Sir,—l have been very much interested and pleased, in reading the accounts in your paper, of the meetings of the Liberal party, during the last few weeks. Judging from the reports that have appeared in the" Examiner." they seem to have been composed of earnest, and, I may say, enthusiastic audiences. The candidate whom they have chosen to champion their cause in the coming struggle is a wise choice.; he has the true ring of a polit- ician about him, a cultured intellect, earnest, and of broad and liberal views.

; The constituency of Warrington is essentially a work inmclass constituency, and the election will mainly I depend upon the votes of that class. It is to them that I wish to address a few words. The time was when they had no votes ? Little more than 20 years have elapsed since the first instalment was granted to them, through the exertions of the Liberal party, led by the : illustrous leader who still lives to lead them, let us hope' togreater victories. But it was not until 1885 that the full enfranchisement of the people was complete ' by an act of that year, piloted by the same great leader. Their position up to 1887 was entirely ignored, and so far as their influence in the election of members of Parlia- ment was concerned they might as well have been denizens af "Darkest Africa." Now all is changed : household suffrage has become the law of the land, and every householder has a vote. Two thirds of the voters are workingmen ; it follows therefore that the power is in their hands, and the next Parliament is what they like to make it! I do not wish to under-rate the work of Parliaments previous to the reform era. They passed many good and useful measures, such as the repeal of the Corn Laws the inauguration of Free Trade, repeal of taxes on knowledge, newspaper stamp duties, and many other measures which have eonferred immense benefits on the nation, measures which were opposed tooth and nail by the Tory party; and not until extreme pressure was put upon them, sometimes by bringing the people to the brink of revolution, did they give way, and allow them to pass. Our methods now are of a different char- acter ; we resort to more peaceful and constitutional ways of making known our wants and our influence felt, namely through the ballot box. I would strongly appeal to the working-men of your town to arouse themselves to a sense of their responsibility in the corn- ing struggle. The next election will be a momentous one, for, losides the Home Rule question, other ques- tions of deep importance to the well being and welfare of the nation will engage the attention of the next Par- liament.

'rho present Government have been in office nearly 21 years, and they have been true as steel to their old traditions, passing bad measures and opposing good ones. They have proved that Tories are Tories still ; and the same old story has to b 3 repeated that, whilst the Liberals trust the people, the Conservatives rule by fear. They concede as little as possible of political power ; their measures even when tin,ed with Liberal ideas are generally marred by checks and counter-checks, so that what they give with the right hand they take away with the left. An examination of some of the Bills passed during their term of office will prove the truth of these asser- tions. 'rake the Coercion Bill, which is of the most infamous description, a bill of eternal duration, or until such time as the Liberals return to power to sweep it away. Then there is the much belauded Land Bill of , Mr. Balfour, which was to turn Ireland into an Eden by I making every peasant his own landlord, wnich from its incongruity has proved a dead letter. Other measures I which they have put their hand upou,such as the Sugar ! Bounties Bill, which sent up the price of that most neces- sary commodity of the poor 25 per cent. ; the wheel tax proposed by their" heaven-born "Chancellor of the Exchequer, a tax which in our large towns would have inflicted grievous burdens upon a class of traders whose struggle for existence is of the most intense kind : and in the last session of this Parliament, they have intro- ' duced a bill f.‘r the Local Government of Ireland, which for mistrust of the people has net been equalled In any previous session, and had this the least chance of becoming law, I should despair of the sister Isle ever receiving justice at the hands of England. Instead of being called the Local Government (Ireland) Bill, it ought to be called the Local Government (Ireland) Cri- minal Procedure Bill. These measures are sufficient to prove that the present occupiers of the Treasury Bench are inimical to the true interests of the masses.

To enumerate all the measures they have opposed would occupy too much of your space : two typical measures will be sufficient to show their hostility. In the early days of the session, a bill was introdued to give power to Bomugh and County Councils to elect a certain number of magistrates, when the whole phalanx of the Tory party were beaten up to oppose so moderate a measure. A session or two ago Mr. Gladstone introduced a Bill to enable a Roman Catholic to occupy the position of Lord Lieutenant of Irelantl, and the Lord Chancellor of Eng- land, and thus remove one of the last rags of religious intolerance and bigotry. But no. the Church was in danger, and the dismemberment of the empire loomed in ! the distance if such became the law of the land ; so the Tories kicked it out. .

Well now, Mr. Editor, all these things your present member has supported and opposed at different times, and the working-classes are asked to send as his successor a man who has promised to adopt the same line of policy; whose ambition is, he says, to " walk in ili3 footsteps," , whose proudest boast is that he is " a good old-fashioned , Tory.' We have been taught the last few years that there were no Tories; that all politicians were of a Liberal hue, the difference being in degree only ; but it appears it is not so ' • there is still one left, and Warrington has been selected as the place of sepulture for the last of that antiquated and fossilized species of politician. I very well remember the first election of the aged baronet—who is retiring into private life, a position he is so well fitted to adorn. I have watched his career in the House, and I have failed to discover any single in- stance in which his voice has been raised on behalf of the oppressed, or a vote given to enhance the interests of the toiling millions of the realm. I do not remember him ever making a speech, proposing a resolution, or even asking a question during the whole of the time he has been your member. Perhaps it is as well that he did none of these things : he might have made a mess of it. No doubt he has looked upon Warrington as a kind of snug borough, with very nice people who never asked any questions as to his duties in Parliament, who never pressed him to give an account of his stewardship, so that he never consulted his constituents or appealed for advice to them on any question that was likely to affect their happiness. Warrington has occupied an ignoble position from this kind of representation; its influence in the political world has been nil, and the electors are asked to perpetuate this ignoble position by electing a good old-fashioned Tory ! I hope the seductive influence of the present member will have no effect in inducing the elec- tors to support a candidate of his own kidney. , It is quite time Warrington shook off the sloth and apathy that has been a distinguishing characteristic of the constituency, and elected a man more abreast of the times, who will aid in retrieving past neglect, and thus ' shake off the taunt that has been applied as being the "sleepy borough." In Dr. Houston the voters have such a man. A man in touch with the people of advanced democratic views, and who is willing and able to give effect to his convictions, who if elected to the House of Commons will adorn it with his eloquence, enrich its morality with his honesty, and by his sets will add to the sum of human happfmess. am thinking, however, that you Liberals of Warring- ton have a tough job before you ; it will require all your energies, all your zeal, all your organisation. Every man must put his shoulder to the wheel, and work as though the election depended upon his individual exer- tions. The enemy will use every means, resort to every trick, fight to the very death to retain their preserit position ; but the Liberals,with the candidate they have selected, united action, and determination have nothing to feu.

In another letter, bi• yLur kind permission, I hope to touch on some of the questions waiting for solution, and which before long must be dealt with. AN OLD WARRINGTONIAN. Birmingham, March Bth, 1892.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 19, 1892.

div.head: BRIMSTOOA.N AN' TRA.YCLE.
div.p: BRIMSTOOA.N AN' TRA.YCLE.
(MIXED.)

Br Timr o' Drc 0' BOB'S. Wod do aw think o' this -Miners' halladay ? A w feel verra strongly on th' question, becose aw lied a empty coyl-hoyle at th' time they went halladayin' an a lot moore fooaks th' same strew-, ; they think same as me, thad is as gas cinders an' borgy are dear at tenpence an' a shillin' a hundred weight—o' ninety peawnd, to say nowt abeawt 'em booath bein' wed l damped. These middlemen want pooin' o'er th' cayls—iv they're to blame ;iv irs between th' maysters an' men they deserve coyls o' fire heeapin' on their heads—metaforickally. Owd King Coyl is a tyrant an' its a theawsand pities he corn'd be dethroned. Yo' corn'd oppen th' papper aytlier mornin' or fleet beawt readin' as this factory an' t'other factory are stopped an' so mony hundred hands are throt eawt; an' its affectin' th' railway companies an' th' ship pin' trade, for accoordire to Wensda's peppers vessels at some o'th' Eastern poorts corn'd ged car- goes, Hartlepool docks bein' deserted. Iv th' hallo- day dofian'd end this week things 'II be geddin' serious for some on us, an' aw darsay we're nod hafe as badly off as th' poor crayters London. Dlooast on us hes heeard o' Colliers' halidays, an' a' lot on us olez imagined thad meant a tooathri on em gooin' i' swell confectioners' shops at th' seea- side to buy a fifty shillin' brides cake to eyt to a gallon o' ale ; or else a ten sbillin' pine-appo at th' fruiterers,'an' avin' heaw id were cooked. An' we've laughed at them buzzes, an' happen believed pert on 'em to be true,but this so o' halladay meks us laugh at th' wrang side ov us face. Aw dorn'd want to give up usin' coy!, becose stoves wi' gas or oil, or owt else, doesu'd look hooamly or gradely ; yo' corn'd stor 'em up wi' a pooaker, yo know, an' yo' corn'd draw reawnd 'em ov a fleet to read a book or tell a buzz. Fancy tellin• th' best buzz ever born th' front of a stove, an' imagine heaw flat id wod be ! But as mich as aw like a bit o' fire as shouldn'd cry mi een up iv some scientifick chap fun eawt heaw to bottle up o' th' heeat o' summer fer winter use ; an' even then th' middleman wod step in wi' his nasty tricks, for th' sake o' mekkin' tooathri' peawnd. Thad idea o' inekkin' use o' th' sooperfluous sum- mer heeat is original—as far as aw know, an' aw mek mi country a present on 't; there's moore in id nor there is tryin' to tawk to th' mon i' th' moon, or findin' eawt perpettywal motion, becose as far as th' lost voila we hey no evidence to show as there is sich a mon, an' as regards th' last we hey id under eawr varra nooases—or at leeast under th'wimmens' nooases.
Let's hooap for th' best. onyway.

Tawkin' abeawt this " bemire" question reminds me ov another "bornin'" question, an' that's juven- ile smookin'. A correspondent i' th' " Manchester Guardian "wants to knows iv nowt con be done to stop id, an' he invites other fooak to ventilate ; he mentions th' conference i' Manchester a tooathri week sin', an' th' propositions med (1) for th' minis- ters an' teychers to discourage an oppooase id, (2) for Board Skoo's to teych th' evils o' th' habit, an' (3) th' passin' ov a Act mekkin' id a punishable offence for anybody under 16 to use bacca, an' to punish them as supplies 'em id. Well, that's a big order, an' mi own opinion is as id'll o' end i' smook—or smookin'. _ _ .

—„— Yo' know it's summat like coourtin', is smookin' —it's nowt nobbut imitation. Th' owdst lad—eigh- teen year owd—sees his dad enjoyin' a whiff, sooa he speculates in a eawtfit ; his younger brother— fifteen—sees an' admires, an' does ditto ; an' so on. deawn to th' youngster just eawt o' hippins an' slavverin' bibs. Th' lasses stert coourtin on th' .same principle, an' when ye' begin to sauce 'em or welt 'em, they say : "Eawr Libby Alice lies a chap," or " Eawr John Thomas snooks." This reform'll hey to be like Charity—idll hey to begin at hooam ; au' nod only as regards smookin', an' coourtin', but drinkin' ;as wed. But wod con yo' expect fro' some o'th' parents? One lot on 'ern are too busy, enjoyin' their own vicious habits to attend to them o' their childer, an' t'other is summat like wod aw wonst mentioned i' th' followin' verses:

• Yo'r lads may booze An' act like foo's, An' endless trouble bring; But yo' o' th' while Say, wi' a smile, "Well, youth mon hey id fling." Till there's sich dads There'll be sich lads To " carry on " full swing; feight an' coss, An' drink—an' woss An' fairly hey their fling. * * *

Just a cherch nooat afoore aw forged. Nowt abeawt disestablishment or disendowment, or th' sale o' livin's ; nor nowt abeawt th' way they gabble through th' psalms (though aw hooap when th' Archbishop o' Canterbury reads this week's Brimstooan he'll give orders for his men nod to rattle through 'em as iv they hed a train to catch, or were freetened o' th' dinner geddin cowd). Nor id isn'd abeawt them as is olez pooin' their watter- bury's eawt as soon as the payson teks his text, just as iv they were givin' him to understnnd as they were thin' him, an wod he on his track iv he dudn'd preych long enough. Nor is id abeawt them as comes in lat, or them as wears creaky shoon. It's abeawt them fooak as save their week's coughin' till service time at th' Sunda' an' geds id off their chests then. An wod coughs they hey, an' wod different ways o' trottin 'em eawt ! Good gracious! Aw neer dud meet wi' owt as ridiculous i' o' nil' life, an' iv one could but fotograff them coughs wi a fonograff it wod be a treeat. Fost ov o' yo'd hear thleawd vul- gar cough ov a tackler—one o' them sooart as welly splits th' bronkial tubes when it's ejected ; then there'd be a volley o' dry coughs an aristocra- tick coughs—them sooart yo' know as is between clearin' th' throoat an summat else aw corn'cl kessen. These wod be followed bi a tooathri miscellaneous coughs, an' then yod hey some assoorted coughs to th' left on yo', coughs to th' reight on yo', coughs to th' front on yo', an' coughs at th' back on yo', volleyin' an, thunderin' ; an' yo'd think yo'd med a mistake an' getten in a Hospital for Diseases of the Chest i'steal ov a cherch. Aw've heeard o' fooak as went to some cherches to scoff an' remainin' to pray. but aw fancy these fooak gooa to pray an' re- main to scoff—beavvt th' "S." These fooak goon to eggsibit their coughs at theayters, too, an' th' solos, duets, an' choruses isn'd appreciated one bit ; they owt to be torned eawt, same as is th' lesser evil— cryin' childer—geds served. Id'll come to this in a bit: A chap as wants to tek a sittin' in a cherch or chapel 'll hey to gooa an' be eggsarnined bi a doctor, an' nod accepted as a member iv he doesn'd pass; that's th' only remedy for th' noosance as aw con suggest, but—as th' Juvenile Smookin' Correspondent says—"an expres- sion of opinion from your readers will,l think,mate- rially help to solve the question."

PETITIONS AGAINST THE NEW BILL. Petitions on behalf of the following have been deposit- ed in the private Bill Office of the House of Lords, pray- ing to be heard by counsel against this Bill when the committee stage is reached :—(l) The Bridgewater Trustees, (2) Sir Humphrey Francis de Trafford, (3) Sir Richard Marcus Brooke, (4) London and North-western and Great Western Railway Companies, and (5) South Lancashire and Cheshire Coal Association and Traders and Freighters.
NEAR THE ROLLIN : A STRUGGLE WITH A TREE. (FROM AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.)

For several months past one of the busiest parts on No. 6 section has been near the river Bollia. Here the steam dredger' Mersey "and four grabs have been in constant work deepening a part of the old river, and opening up a new piece of ground leading to the cutting beyond, which is nearly completed and which will form the future canal. For seine few days past the work has been rather retarded, and last week an oak tree of fairly good dimensions was forcibly torn from its long resting place to in.tke way for the dredger. On Tuesday last it was felt that another obstacle was in the way and that it must be removed. The services of " Sandy " the diver were called into requisition and he discovered at a depth of 24 feet, and from 20 to 30 yards from the old river, another gigantic tree. To this the nips were fastened, and by the aid of the dredger's gearing was lifted about a foot from its bed. Again the diver I descended and placed a strong chain around it, to this another chain was fastened and taken to land. This latter chain was attached to the loco " Severn," one of the most powerful engines on the section, and the tug of war commenced, but the tree was too much for the loco ; it moved not budge. Another engine—the " Mammoth" equal to the " Severn " in power was hooked on, and both engines tried to move the monster, but for a while it defied them. Mr. Ewart the agent, who was present on the dredger sent the roperunner to fetch a third engine; but whilst he was on his way another mighty effort was made by the two engines, and the tree was moved. It was drawn through the water

and brought to land. It was found to be four feet I through, and about 20 feet long. How this massive monster came there—who knows ? The course of the river may have changed, but is it possible that a tree of such dimensions would travel far before embedding itself ? And if grown in the immediate district, there must be vast climatic changes, for the oak is anything but indigenous to the neighbourhood to-day. A few gnarled, stunted, apologies for the oak only are visible. Undoubtedly many centuries have passed since the great oak tree found its Lodging place ; but judging from appearance, the bark being fresh and natural as ever, only a few years might have elapsed since it afforded both shelter and shade as a king of the forest.
• WATERMEN'S AND PORTERS' ASSOCIATION AND - • --
THE CANAL COMPANY.
The following correspondence has been published : (Copy.) Druids' Cross, Wavertree,,,l.iverpool, 22nd December,

1891. Dear Lord Egerton,—Complaint has been made to me by Mr. Ellis Gatley, of Runcorn, secretary of the Water- men's and Porters' Association, that he is not allowed to enter the premises of the Manchester Ship Canal Com- pany to see the members of his Association trading on the Bridgewater Canal and the Ship Canal. As it is a matter of common knowledge that the condition of these vratermen leaves much to be desired, and being convinc- ed that the influence of the Association represented by Mr. Gatley is exceedingly wholesome, I venture to place Ins complaint before you. Mr. Gatley applied to Mr. W. H. Collier for the required permission, and was refused it by a letter from the latter gentleman, dated the 6th of August last. Evidence with regard to the hours of work and with regard to the condition generally of the water- men within the area of the operations of the Association named, has been prepared for and accepted on behalf of the B Committee of the Royal Commission on Labour. Flaying read that evidence, I am of opinion that it would be a matter for great 'regret if the Manchester Ship Canal Company should persist is an attitude of antagonism to this Association, and sincerely trust that you will agree with me. I have advised Mr. Gatley to lay his case before the members of the Royal Commission in case the permission he seeks is still refused to him. In case of an unfavourable response from you, but only in such case, I propose to send a copy of this letter and of your reply to the press.—Yours faithfully-, (Signed) Jonm T. BRUNNER. The Lord Egerton of 'Patton. 'Patton Park, Knutsford, December 23rd, 1891.

My dear sir,—l will refer yeur letter of the 22nd inst. to the Bridgewater Committee of the Ship Canal Com- pany, and let you know the answer.—Yours faithfully, (Signed) EGERTON OF TATTON. 1 John T. Brunner, Esq., M.P. 'Patton Park, Knutsford, December 30th, 1891. My dear sir,—l have laid before the Bridgewater Corn- mittee of the Ship Canal Company your letter, and they see no reason for departing from the usual rules of ex- cluding persons not conducting business with the Com- pany from the premises in the case of Mr. Gatley, who is the secretary of a watermen's trade union. Your letter assumes that the object of the Association which Mr. Gatley represents is only to improve the condition of the waterman ; our experience is that it has other objects, which do not equally commend themselves to the Company. If the acquisition of information as to the hours of work and general condition of the water- men, to be laid before the Royal Commissioners on Labour, be the object of Mr. Gatley's request, he can be furnished with these at the offices of the Company at any time. I assume that the object of your letter is of philanthropic character, and therefore answer it with- out prejudice.—l am, yours faithfully, (Signed) EGERTON OF TATTON. J. T. Brunner, Esq., M.P. Druid's Cross, Wavertree Liverpool, 4th January, 1892. Dear Lord Egerton,—Through absence from home your courteous letter of the 30th ult., only came into me hands late on Friday evening. When writing on the 22nd I was fully conscious of the fact that the Association re- presented by Mr. Gatley is a Trade Union with the ordinary objects of a Trade Union. These objects are, I consider, very fairly summed up when described as an endeavour to " impreve the condition" of the members of the Union, and I gather that so far they commend themselves to the Company. I cannot conceive that this particular trade union has any other objects. I presume that your statement that the experience of the Company is that it has " other important objects which do not equally commend themselves to the Company "is tanta- mount to saying that it has adoped improper means for the advancement of its object. If this is the fact, I would be the last man to support them in their action. May I ask if this is your meaning ? I greatly doubt whether the Company can enlighten Mr. Gatley upon the question of the hours of work and general condition of the water- men, and think it exceedingly likely, on the other hand, that the Company would learn much from Mr. Gatley if they consulted him in a kindly spirit. It is my experi- ence that secretaries of trade unions know much more of such matters than do large employers. If, on inquiry, you find that the Upper Mersey Watermen and Porters' Association have not used any improper means I trust that you will recommend the Bridgewater Committee to accede to Mr. Gatley's request. I renew my appeal to you solely because I have been so much impressed by the painful statements made to me by Mr. Gatley, con- firming as they do much of what I have heard and read for years past as to the condition of the canal popula- tion.—Yours faithfully, (Signed) JOHN T. BRUNNER. The Lord Egerton of Tatton. Manchester Ship Canal, 41, Spring-gardens. Manchester, 12th Jan. My dear sir,—l have laid your letter of the 4th Jan. before the Board. I did notin my previous letter in- tend, by using the words "other important objects," to suggest that the trades union you refer to had adopted improper means for the advancement of its object, and I do not think it is a fair construction to place upon the words I used. To give the permission you ask would involve an alteration in the regulations of the Company which the Board is not prepared to recommend, and I must, therefore, adhere to the decision which I have al- ready communicated to you.—My dear sir, yours faith- fully, (Signed) EGERTON OF TATTON. J. T. Brunner, 1,,M .P.

div.head: BREACH OF PROMISE.
div.p: BREACH OF PROMISE.

In the Sheriff's Court, at Manchester, on Thursday, Miss Douglas, daughter of Mr. J. Douglas, Lagos Villas, Guest-road, Prestwich, was awarded £3OO damages against the Rev. William Smethurst Naylor, curate of St. Andrew's, Burnley, for breach of promise of mar- riage.

div.head: LANCASHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL.
div.p: LANCASHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL.

The newly-elected County Council of Lancashire met at the County Hall? Preston, on Wednesday. The,Right Hon. J. T. Hibbert was unanimously re-elected chair- man of the Council. In accepting the office Mr. llibbert expressed the opirdon that, during the first three years of its existence, the Council had done work of great use- fulnees for the county. Since the passing of the Local Government Act, new powers had been given to County Councils, and his impression was that as time went on still greater powers would be entrusted to them. Mr. Hibbert further urged that in the matter of the promo- tion of Bills in Parliament the County Council should he placed on the same level as municipalities. After Mr. bbert's address the Council proceeded to the election of aldermen and the appointment of committees.

The greatest theatre goers in the House of Commons are Mr. T. H. Bolton, Mr. Dickson Hartland, and M. Woodall, and these gentlemen have been nominated to serve on the Select Committee on theatres and variety houses.

div.head: FOUR CHILDREN BURNED TO DEATH.
div.p: FOUR CHILDREN BURNED TO DEATH.

On Monday, Dr. Rowlands, the coroner, held an in- quest on the bodies of the four children who were burned to death on Sunday, at Llanelly. During the evidence of Lewis, the father, and his son, both of whom sobbed bitterly, the jury showed considerable emotion. A ver- dict of accidental death was returned. The mother lies in a precarious condition. The sonj,so dangerously burned is not expected to recover.

div.head: DISPUTE AT BURTONWOOD CHURCH. .
div.p: THE DISPUTE AT BURTONWOOD CHURCH. .

Matters at Burtonwood Church, do not appear to improve. On Sunday afternoon the Vicar again un- dertook the task of collecting the offertory, remark- ing before doing so, that he would not ask anybody to do it, and then there would be no stones thrown. The wardens still maintain a defiant attitude, and in reply to the Vicar's "Lenten Pastoral" extracts from which we published last week, have issued to the parishioners of Burtonwood,a contradiction to the whole of the Vicar's statements. In their reply they commence by saying—" A circular has been sent round the parish as a kind of "Lenten Pastoral " by the Vicar,the Rev. A. M. Mitchell, in which he publicly denounces the con- dition of the church. As these statements are calculated to reflect discredit on the churchwardens' who have laboured and persevered, with the kind help of the parishioners, for the last three years, to make the church more comfortable, and of this we leave you to judge for yourselves." They then go on to point out, in refutation of the statements of the Vicar, that three years ago they had a new roof put on the church at a cost of £3oo,and maintain that it is perfectly weather-proof, and that there is no indication of the rain beating in as alleged by the Vicar. They state that a new roof was put on the vestry, and that the interior was beautified and made very comfortable. They then proceed to contradict the Vicar's statement that the "wretched and miser- able " condition of the church has been the means of reducing the congregation. They state that the reason of the decrease in the numbers attending is due simply to the fact of the parishioners having no voice in the appointment of the Vicar, and because they are asked to .submit to a form of worship that is quite foreign to the worshippers. They affirm that the church was never more comfortable in the recollection of any parishioner than at the present time, so that its wretched condition cannot account for the poor congregation. In conclu- sion they say that had the Vicar accepted their offer, he would have known most if not all of the parishioners within the first week of his taking charge of such a neglected, wretched, and miserable church. The cir- cular is signed by Thos. Howard and John Fairclough as churchwardens.

div.head: CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL ITEMS.
div.p: CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL ITEMS.

The first meeting of the re-elected Cheshire County Council was held on Thursday. Mr. Duncan Graham was unanimously re-elected Chairman, on the motion of the Duke of Westminster, seconded by Mr. J. Beckett; and Mr. James Tomkinson was also re-appointed vice-Chairman without opposi- tion.

The compact lytween the two political parties as to the election of aldermen was kept in good faith, and the retiring aldermen, who are all Liberals with the excep- tion of Mr. Webb, were re-elected as follows :—Messrs. James Tomkinson, Wellington Hall •, Francis Wm. Webb, Crewe; Thomas Collier, Alderley Edge ; Thomas Rigby, Sutton Weaver ; Alexander Bedwell, Wilmslow ; James Smith, New Brighton ; David Basil Hewitt, Northwich ; Thomas Beeley, Birkenhead; Samuel Hodgkinson, Margie; Henry Nield, Higher Whitley. The Committee to consider the proposed Vehicular Bridge across the Mersey, to connect Runcorn and Wid- nes, was again appointed, but there was an alteration in the names, which are as follows :—Alderman Joseph Verdin, D. B. Hewitt, Ralph Bates. and Thomas Beeley ; Councillors Stanton Eddowes, Thos. Parker, Charles Welch, Philip Speakman, and Charles W. Hazlehurst. Both the local members were re-appointed to the various Committees on which they had previously served, and Mr. Speakman was also selected for duty on the Parliamentary- Committee, one of the most useful and important Committees of the Council. The Council, for a technical reason, could not accede to the request of the Runcorn Commissioners and take over as a main road the road from the boundary of Hal- ton to the Railway Station over Waterloo Bridge,but, on , the motion of Mr. Beckett, the Chairman of the High- ways Committee, the Council have conceded what is of equal benefit. It was decided on Thursday that the Council contribute, until it otherwise orders the sum of £203 per annum to the Runcorn Improvement Com- missioners towards the cost of the maintenance, repair, enlargemmt, and improvement of the road, subject to the thoroughfare being kept in repair to the satisfaction of the County Surveyor. Mr. Speak- man who is a member of the Main Roads Committeethas worked hard for some time to secure this concession,and we congratulate him upon the result of his labours. The 'contribution is equal to £5,000 capitalised at four per cent, and should enable the Board of Commissioners to ' devote a greater portion of our local rate to other thoroughfares which are sadly in need of repair. Now that Runcorn have received £2OO for Technical In- struction,s.nd £2OO for a main road,it is to be hoped that Mr. Speakman will still further use his influence on the Technical Instruction Committee and obtain a good building grant towards the proposed Technical Institute.

div.head: CADISHEAD,
div.p: CADISHEAD,

TEMPERANCE. ENTERTAINMENT..—OH Saturday evening, a temperance entertainment waS held in the Wesleyan Schoolroom. Mr. G. Hesford gave a short address. The meeting was also addressed by Mr. Barry, of Man- chester. Mr. G. Whitfield presided. A collection was made at the close to defray expenses. CADISHEAD CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL.— A public tea meeting, cDnducted by men only, was held in the above place on Saturday evening. There was a good attend- ance. After tea the evening was enlivened by songs from Mr. F. Marshall and Mr. R. Lone; recitations from Mr. Sudan and Mr. Hazlehurst ; readings from Mr. R. Williams and Mr. N. Whitfield ; and addresses from the Rev. J. Crewe (chairman), Mr. J. A. Wright, and Mr. Wilson. Votes of thanks were proposed by Mrs. Ander- son, and seconded by Mrs. Bailey, for the excellent man- ner in which the gentlemen had conducted tile proceed- ings.

div.head: I BOXING AfATOII BETWEEN WARRING-
div.p: I BOXING AfATOII BETWEEN WARRING-
TON MEN.

A boxing match took place on Thursday evening, at Meadow's Boxing Club, Liverpool, between two well-known local athletes named Allen and Fair. The contest was for a medal, and, as showing the interest taken in the event, it may be mentioned that nearly one hundred persons went from Warrington, and paid the charges for admission (Sc.) to witness it. It is described by those who were present as having been a very spirited encounter, extending into a tenth round. At the commencement Fair seems to have had the best of matters and 2oored his antagonist on more than one occasion. As time wore on, however, and one round succeeded another, the heavier weight and staying powers of Allen began to tell their tale and Fair showed more obvious signs of exhaustion, though he continued to make a plucky stand. The tenth round saw the finale, which came in the shape of a swinging blow which caught Fair under the ear, and completely incap- acitated him from coming up to time. No injuries were sustained kv the combatants beyond some slight bruises and swellings.
COUNCILLOR BOLTON ON " ODONTO- GLOSSUMS."

On Saturday week Councillor Bolton, of Warring- ton, read a paper before the Chester Paxton Society of Gardners on " Odontogloesums," which are a variety of orchid flowers, in the growing of which Mr. Bolton has been very successful at his new residence at Wilderspool. The "Gardening world" of study last gives a report of. the first part of the paper. In the course of his address Councillor Bolton pointed out that the flowers he was dealing with were in shape as like butterflies as a flower could be. They were a sort that needed special treatment as they were natives of forests which were teeming with moisture, and therefore the atmoepliere of the greenhouse had to be kept up to a certain amount of saturation, else the flowers would not grow. They also required to be kept rather cool at night, a temperature of from 40 to 50 degrees being suffi- cient, but in the day-time it should be allowed to get slighly higher by the heat of the sun. Some of the varieties required, however, rather more warmth than that. Mr. Bolton also gave a full des- cription of the insect pests that infested the flower, and detailed his own experience in dealing with them. The paper was much appreciated by those present at the. meeting, and after he had replied to sundry questions, be was accorded:a hearty vote of thanks on the motion of Mr. John Taylor, the president of the Society.

THE RAINHILL TRAGEDIES.
(Continued front page 3). INQUEST CN THE VICTIMS.

Drs. Hutchinson and M'Lellan, of Widnes, made a post mortent examination of the bodies yesterday morning. Their task was a fearful one, silo!' as the profession are but seldom called upon to perform. There was a groat crowd of people round Dinham Villa shortly before twelve o'clock. The police refused to allow admittance to any person owing to the post-mortem examination of the victims which was going on. The brother of Deeming, who is the very image of the mur- derer, was greatly distressed, and appeared hardly able to control his feelings. THE INQUEST.

The inquest into the deaths of Mrs. Marie Deeming and her four children was opened yesterday by Mr. S. Brig- house, county coroner, at the Victoria Hotel, Rainhill. The names and ages of the deceased children are Bertha, nine, Marie, seven, Sydney Francis, five' and Lila, eighteen months. Mrs. Deeming was aged thirty-nine years. The jury left the Victoria Hotel shortly before one to view the bodies, arriving at the entrance to Dinham Villa about ten minutes past. The bedies were lying in separate coffins as the jury entered the door, the mother towards the centre, the coffin of the youngest child being placed at her left side and close to. The lids of the coffins were all standing up against the wall, and one of them bore the following affecting inscription:—" Jesus Christ called a little child (Matilda Deeming, aged two years) unto him." The lettering was in yellow upon a plain black shield. The coffins had the appearance in some instances of being almost empty. the bodies had so shrunk. The children especially had shrivelled up to dwarfish semblance. The jurymen carefully approached, took a hurried glimpse at the remains, and rushed I downstairs, doing the hest they could to get rid of the painful sensations they had experienced. Upon the inquiry being resumed the coroner, address- ing the jury, said their duty was very simple. It was suggestive that the bodies were those of Frederick Bayley Deetning's wife and children, and that they had come by their deaths by his hands ; and further, that he was responsible for the acts lie had committed on them. There was no suggestion that any other person had had anything to do with their deaths, and conse- quently their duty was simplified to a great extent. Be asked them to disabuse their minds of anything they had read in the papers. Evidence was then educed ak followe

Albert Deeming said : ,1 live in Canning-st., Birken- head, and am a fitter. I first saw the bodies at Dinham Villa yesterday morning, and at once identified the re- mains as those of my brother Frederick Bayley Deem- ing's wife and four children. My sister-in-law was about thirty-nine years of age, and I last saw her alive last July. She was then staying at my house,where she ha,.. been for two years. In that month she and her children went to join ha brother at 'Wadil in order to complete arrangements prior to sailing for California. The witness at this point sobbed bitterly, and exclaimed : " I knew this seven months ago. I saw it in my dreams." After leaving my house I never saw her again alive. At that time slip had about £lOO. My brother visited us twice after that, and each time said my sister-in-law and chil- dren were staying at Brighton. In reply to a question I asked him as to what lie was doing, lie said he was about to go on an exploring expedition to the Argen- tine Republic. By a Juryman : My brother was never married before his union with the deceased: Ile described himself as a seaman.
Walter Deeming corroborated his brother's evidence of identification.

By the police : When he saw his brother in Hull he was in custody on some charge. Frederick at one time lived in Bridge-st., Birkenhead, with his wife, and they seemed to live happily together. Inspector George Pattinsen, of Widnes, said in accor- dance with instructions, he went with a detachment of police to Dinham Villa on the 18th. The throats of the mother and three children had been cut, while Bertha had been strangled. Bertha's head was covered with a towel, and a rope was round her neck. All the chil- dren's heads were covered with something. Mrs. Deem- mg was tied round ber legs an neck with an eiderdown quilt. The woman was only partly dressed, and had two rings on her marriage finger. All the bodies were laid lengthways, the hole being between five and six feet long. It was evident that eemeat had been put at the bottom and round the sides before they had been put in.
Police-sergeant Chipchase, who assisted in the excava- tion, corroborated the last witness, and said two of the children's hands were tied behind them.
Dr. McClellan, Widnes, and Dr. Hutchinson gave evi- dence, and the inquest was adjourned.

TERRIBLE FIRE IN LONDON.—FIVE LIVES LOST About four o'clock yesterday morning a disastrous fire, resulting in the death of four persons, occurred on the premises of Mr. J. Weston, butcher, Lillie-rd., Fulham. Mr. and Mrs. Weston, two daughters, and a servant named Amy Glover were sleeping on the premises. Mr. Weston rushed downstairs on the first alarm, and the flames bursting through the staircase prevented his return. By the time the firemen had arrived the inside of the house was like a furnace, and Mrs. Weston, her daughters, and the servant were burnt to death. There were other occupants of the house who got out, includ- ing Weston's sister, who has since died from her burns. THE MINERS' HOLIDAY.' MEETING OF THE FEDERATION. It was decided at the Miners' Conference at West- minster, yesterday, that the miners on resuming should work five days a week. This resolution will come into force on April 11, Monday being a general weekly holiday. . -
- Prices are falling. Since last Friday the London market has declined 103. EXTINSION OF THZ DURHAM STRIKII. _

A Durham correspondent telegraphs :—The strikers were to-day reinforced by 10,000 miners from unassoci- ated collieries, who notices have expired, and who have brought their gear to the hank. Numerous cases of dis- order have been reported to the police. '
We understand that all, or nearly all, of the mon thrown out of employment in Warrington in consequence of the miners' strike, will resume work on Monday.
YESTERD kY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LOBOS.
Tim Lord Chancellor took his seat at a quarter past four.

The Earl of Westmoreland took the oath, and his seat in succession. Millbank Prison 13ill passed through Committee; the Clergy Discipline Bill and Bridges (Scot- land) Act Amendment Bill were read a third time.
The House adjourned at twenty minutes to five. HOUSE OF CONIMONS.

FINANCIAL BUSINESS.—Mr. BALFOUR moved that at to-night's sitting. financial business Should be entered on at any hour. Mr. Sexton opposed the motion and moved to limit the application of the resolution to the present financial year ; but the motion was defeated i by 187 to 91. Mr. Balfour's motion was carried by 208 to 129.

PPLY.—The House went into Committee of Supply, and considerablo discussion ensued on the vote on ac- count of over three millions. A motion to report pro- gress was defeated by 202 to 127. Afterwards Mr. Bat- Foun moved that the question be now put, but the Chairman declined to put closure motion, and suggested that the motion for reduction of the vote should be with- drawn. (Cries of "No, no.") The Committee divided on proposed reduction of the vote ; ayes 118; noes 194. The sitting was then suspended.

COUNTY OF CHESTER. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the next GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for the COUNTY OF CHESTER will be held at the COURT HOUSE, NETHER KNUTSFORD, in the said County on MONDAY, the 4th day of April next, at half-past eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hundreds of Bucklow, Macclesfield, and Northwich, forming the Knutsford District, and the trials of all prisoners com- mitted from such Hundreds, will take place at such Sessions. The Graind and Petty Jury for the Knutsford District must be in attendance at the Court House, Knutsford, at the opening of the Court on MONDAY, the 4th day of April next, at half-past eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. THE Court will be Adjourned to the Castle of Chester on THURSDAY, the 7th day of April next, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hundreds of Braxton, Eddisbury, Nantwich, and Wirral, forming the Chester District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from the last-men- tioned Hundreds will take place at such Adjourned Ses- sions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Chester Dis- trict must be in attendance at the Castle of Chester at the opening of the Court on THURSDAY, the 7th day of April next, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk of the Peace. Chester, 14th March, 1892.

Gentlemen,—l have now had your Marsh's Patent Smoke- oonsuming Stove for 18 months in constant use, and the longer we use it the better we like it, and for cleanliness aud comfort it is a great contrast to the open fire. I was rather sceptical in regard to its not requiring the chimney sweep- ing, but having watched it very carefully for over 12 months, 1 ROI now satbiled that it does all that, your advertisement says it will do, for I have not had the chimney swept since It was put in. and it keeps its draught ; and so I find that not only does it save fuel, but the dirt, cost, and inconvenience of the sweep.—Yours truly, JOHN A. THISTLETHWAITE. 322, Leeds Road, Bradford, January 15, 1892. Gentlemen,—/ have two of your Marsh's Patent Smoke consuming and Fuel-economising Fires at work continuously in my establishment. One fire has been Axed for fourteer months, working two large ovens (one heavy cast iron and one sheet iron), and the other is applied to a complete bakers range, with large ovens, side boiler, and hot plate, and they have both given every satisfaction. After getting the fires well started with nuts, we use practically nothing but smudge on the two-decker, and nuts and smudge on the range, for the remainder of the day. The heat, obtained from this inferior coal with this Patent fire is really marvellous ; indeed, one ' can hardly realise tile fact of being able to bake bread and pastry with common smudge. Previous to having these Fires we had to swet.p the chimney every two months, but it is now fourteen months since we had It swept, and so far as I can judge, there will never be any necessity to sweep it again.—Yours truly, t TRELFA.
